definition: Involving reasoning from facts or particulars to general principles or from effects to causes.
example: A posteriori demonstration.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā posteriōrī (“involving reasoning from effect to cause, from experience to theory”, literally “from what follows”).

definition: A kind of hemp obtained from the abaca plant in the Philippines.
etymology: From Spanish abacá, from Tagalog abaka.

definition: At or near or toward the stern of a ship or tail of an airplane.
example: Ships with square sails sail fairly efficiently with the wind abaft.
etymology: From Middle English obaft, baft, baften, from Old English beæftan; be (“by”) (modern English by) + æftan (“behind”) (modern English after). See also aft.

definition: Feeling or caused to feel ill at ease or self-conscious or ashamed.
example: Felt abashed at the extravagant praise.

definition: At right angles to the length of a ship or airplane.
etymology: From a- (“in the direction of”) + beam (“keel”).

definition: A poplar that is widely cultivated in the United States; has white bark and leaves with whitish undersurfaces.
etymology: From Middle English abelle, albell, aubel, from Old French aubel, aubiel, from Medieval Latin albellus (“white poplar”), diminutive of Latin albus (“white”). Some forms after Middle Dutch abeel, from Old French.

definition: In a hopeless resigned manner.
example: She shrugged her shoulders abjectly.
etymology: From Middle English abjectli (“with great humility”), from abject (“outcast, rejected; wretched; humble, lowly; of poor quality, worthless; menial”) + -li (suffix forming adverbs); analysable as abject + -ly.

definition: A disavowal or taking back of a previous assertion.
etymology: First attested around 1439. From Middle English abjuracioun, from Latin abiūrātiō (“forswearing, abjuration”), from ab (“from, away from”) + iūrō (“swear or take an oath”), from iūs (“law, right, duty”).

definition: Formally reject or disavow a formerly held belief, usually under pressure.
example: She abjured her beliefs.
etymology: From Late Middle English abjuren (“to give up (something);

definition: In an offensive and hateful manner.
example: I don't know anyone who could have behaved so abominably.

definition: Reduce in scope while retaining essential elements.
example: He had his rights abridged by the crooked sheriff.
etymology: From Middle English abreggen, abregge, abrigge (“curtail, lessen”), from Old French abregier, abreger, from Late Latin abbreviō, abbreviāre (“make brief”). Doublet of abbreviate.

definition: A shortened version of a written work.
A shortened version of a written work.
example: An abridgment of pleasures or of expenses.
etymology: First attested in 1494. From Middle English abrygement, from Middle French abrégement. Equivalent to abridge + -ment.

definition: An instance of sudden interruption.
etymology: From abrupt + -ion. From Latin abruptio, from abrumpo (“to break off”).

definition: (mountaineering) a descent of a vertical cliff or wall made by using a doubled rope that is fixed to a higher point and wrapped around the body.
etymology: From German abseilen, from ab- (“down”) + Seil (“rope”).

definition: In an absentminded or preoccupied manner.
example: He read the letter absently.

definition: The property of being absorbent.
Having power or capacity or tendency to absorb or soak up something (liquids or energy etc.).
example: As absorbent as a sponge.

definition: In an abusive manner.
example: He behaved abusively toward his children.

definition: The act of giving special importance or significance to something.
The use or application of an accent; the relative prominence of syllables in a phrase or utterance.
etymology: From Late Latin accentuatio. Compare French accentuation. Equivalent to accentuate + -ion.

definition: Adaptation to a new climate (a new temperature or altitude or environment).
Get used to a certain climate.
example: They never acclimatized in Egypt.

definition: Get used to a certain climate.
example: They never acclimatized in Egypt.

definition: A musician who plays the accordion.
Speak to someone.
example: A beggar accosted me as soon as I stepped outside.
etymology: From Middle French accoster, acoster, from Old French acoster (“to stand beside”) (whence Medieval Latin accostare), from Old French a- + coste (“side, flank”).

definition: Marked or produced by accretion.
Increasing by successive addition.
example: The eventual accumulative effect of these substances.

definition: In an accusing manner.
example: He looked at her accusingly.

definition: Not made up of or divided into cells.
example: Acellular background is that which is still present when the cells are removed from the microscope.

definition: The cup-shaped hollow in the hipbone into which the head of the femur fits to form a ball-and-socket joint.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin acētābulum (“vinegar saucer, ¹⁄₄₈ congius”), from acētum (“vinegar”) + -bulum (“-bule: a vessel for”).

definition: Having no hue.
example: Achromatic color scheme.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀχρωμάτιστος (akhrōmátistos, “uncolored”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”), equivalent to a- + chromatic; compare French achromatique.

definition: A color lacking hue; white or grey or black.
A color lacking hue; white or grey or black.
A compound lens system that forms an image free from chromatic aberration.
Vision using the rods.
A bacterium that is used to make yogurt and to supplement probiotics.
Milk fermented by bacteria; used to treat gastrointestinal disorders.
Any of various usually poisonous plants of the genus Aconitum having tuberous roots and palmately lobed leaves and blue or white flowers.
Either of the passages in the outer ear from the auricle to the tympanic membrane.

Enlargement of bones of hands and feet and face; often accompanied by headache and muscle pain and emotional disturbances; caused by overproduction of growth hormone by the anterior pituitary gland (due to a tumor).
etymology: From French acromégalie, from New Latin acromegalia, from Ancient Greek ἄκρον (ákron, “tip, extremity”) and μέγας (mégas, “large”). By surface analysis, acro- + -megaly.

definition: Relating to or exhibiting actinism.
example: In medicine, actinic keratoses usually occur in sundamaged skin and exhibit hyperkeratosis.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀκτίς, ἀκτῖν- (aktís, aktîn-, “ray”) + -ic.

definition: Dermatitis caused exposure to sunlight.
Electromagnetic radiation that can produce photochemical reactions.
Electromagnetic radiation that can produce photochemical reactions.
Any of a series of radioactive elements with atomic numbers 89 through 103.
(chemistry) a series of 15 radioactive elements with increasing atomic numbers from actinium to lawrencium.
Causing motion or action or change.
Activity that transgresses moral or civil law.
etymology: From Late Latin āctus reus (“guilty act”), from Latin āctus (“act”) + reus (“guilty”); after Late Latin and English mens rea.

definition: (of a leaf shape) narrowing to a slender point.
example: Acuminate leaves, teeth, etc.
etymology: First attested in 1611; borrowed from Latin acuminātus, perfect passive participle acuminō (“to sharpen to a point”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: A leaf narrowing to a slender point.
A sensitivity that is keen and highly developed.
example: Dogs have a remarkable acuteness of smell.

definition: Without advance preparation.
example: He spoke ad lib.

definition: In proportion to the estimated value of the goods taxed.
example: The goods were taxed ad valorem.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ad valorem (“by value”).

definition: (physiology) moving of a body part toward the central axis of the body.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin adductio, adductionis, from adducō (“to bring to oneself”), from ad + ducō (“to lead”). Compare French adduction. Equivalent to adduct + -ion or adduce + -tion. See adduce.

definition: Relating to or resembling lymphatic glands or lymphoid tissue.
etymology: Late 19th century borrowing from French adénoïde, from New Latin adenoīdēs, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓δενοειδής (ădenoeidḗs, “glandular”), from ᾰ̓δήν (ădḗn, “gland”) + -ο- (-o-) + -ειδής (-eidḗs, “-oid, -like”);

definition: A waxy mineral that is a mixture of hydrocarbons and occurs in association with petroleum; some varieties are used in making ceresin and candles.
Having the property of containing fat.
example: He recommended exercise to reduce my adiposity.
etymology: From adipose + -ity, from Latin adeps (“fat, lard”).

definition: Lie adjacent to another or share a boundary.
example: Canada adjoins the U.S.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman adjoindre, from Latin adiungō.

definition: Concerned with adjudicating.
Work in an administrative capacity; supervise or be in charge of.
example: Administer a program.
etymology: * archaic: Latin administrātus, past participle of administrō. * modern: Back-formation from administration (from Latin administrātiō, also from administrō) (The exact etymology is disputed, see note below.)

definition: Extreme attractiveness.
With adoration.
example: He looked at his wife adoringly.

definition: Accumulate (liquids or gases) on the surface.
example: The gas was purified by adsorbing the impurities onto active carbon.
etymology: From French adsorber, from Latin ad- (“to”) + sorbeō (“suck in”).

definition: (meteorology) the horizontal transfer of heat or other atmospheric properties.
etymology: From Latin advectio (“act of bringing”), from advectus (past participle of advehere (“to carry to”), from ad- + vehere (“to convey”)) + -io.

definition: Associated by chance and not an integral part.
example: They had to decide whether his misconduct was adventitious or the result of a flaw in his character.

definition: Root growing in an unusual location e.g. from a stem.
Willing to undertake or seeking out new and daring enterprises.
example: Adventurous pioneers.

definition: A woman adventurer.
etymology: From adventure (verb) + -ess, after adventurer. Compare earlier governess, sorceress, etc.

definition: Recklessness in politics or foreign affairs.
An advertisement that is written and presented in the style of an editorial or journalistic report.
With intention; in an intentional manner.
The right in English law of presenting a nominee to a vacant ecclesiastical benefice.
etymology: From Middle English avowson, from Anglo-Norman avouson, from Latin advocātiō. Doublet of advocation.

definition: An edge tool used to cut and shape wood.
Expose to fresh air.
example: Aerate your old sneakers.
etymology: From Latin aer (“air”) + English -ate. Compare French aérer.

definition: An apparatus for exposing something to the air (as sewage).
example: Faucet aerator.

definition: A device that provides reactive force when in motion relative to the surrounding air; can lift or control a plane in flight.
A synthetic porous ultralight material derived from a gel, in which the liquid component of the gel has been replaced with a gas.
example: The microscope collects stacks of digital images of the aerogel collectors in the array.

definition: Of or relating to aviation medicine.
Of or pertaining to aeronautics.
In the form of ultramicroscopic solid or liquid particles dispersed or suspended in air or gas.
The cause of a disease.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin aetiologia. By surface analysis, aetio- + -logy. Doublet of aetiologia.

definition: A disposition to be friendly and approachable (easy to talk to).
An inability to understand the consequences of one's actions because of financial privilege.
A potent carcinogen from the fungus Aspergillus; can be produced and stored for use as a bioweapon.
Excited in anticipation.
With planning and intention.
example: With malice aforethought.

definition: An image (usually a negative image) that persists after stimulation has ceased.
Small terrestrial lizard of warm regions of the Old World.
etymology: Borrowed from Sranan Tongo agama (“lizard”), borrowed from a Gbe language. Compare Ewe agama (“chameleon”).

definition: Imperfect development; nondevelopment of a part.
A clumping of bacteria or red cells when held together by antibodies (agglutinins).
etymology: Multiple origins. The oldest usage, in relation to tissues adhering or healing in medical contexts, appears in the 16th century, from French agglutination.

definition: Expressing pain or agony.
example: Agonized screams.

definition: Of or relating to the athletic contests held in ancient Greece.
Agile long-legged rabbit-sized rodent of Central America and South America and the West Indies; valued as food.
etymology: From French agouti, from Old Tupi akuti. The name of the acouchi is probably from the same source.

definition: Someone concerned with the science or art or business of cultivating the soil.
A fit of shivering or shaking.
example: Fever and ague.

definition: Colicroot having a scurfy or granuliferous perianth and white flowers; southeastern United States.
Colicroot having a scurfy or granuliferous perianth and white flowers; southeastern United States.
Gentian of eastern North America having clusters of bristly blue flowers.
A memorandum summarizing the items of an agreement (used especially in diplomatic communications).
Transport (cargo) by air.
A gun that propels a projectile by compressed air.
In a flippant manner.
example: This cannot be airily explained to your children.

definition: Medium for radio and television broadcasting.
example: The president used the airwaves to take his message to the people.

definition: (of aircraft) fit to fly.
example: An airworthy helicopter...

definition: Of or relating to the axil.
Needless warnings.
A tavern where ale is sold.
etymology: From Middle English alehous, alehuse from Old English ealuhūs. By surface analysis, ale + house.

definition: An obsolete kind of container used for distillation; two retorts connected by a tube.
etymology: From French alambic, from Medieval Latin alembīcus, from Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup, cap of a still”). Doublet of ambix and lambic.

definition: Flesh of shad-like fish abundant along the Atlantic coast or in coastal streams.
A green variety of chrysoberyl used as a gemstone.
etymology: From Alexander + -ite, named after Alexander II of Russia.

definition: A psychiatrist and specialist in the legal aspects of mental illness.
etymology: Borrowed from French aliéniste, from aliéné (“insane”).

definition: Signifying an exact divisor or factor of a quantity.
etymology: From French aliquote, from Latin aliquot.

definition: An integer that is an exact divisor of some quantity.
example: 4 is an aliquot part of 12.

definition: A series of non-aromatic saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH(2n+2).
example: The carbon chain of an alkane may be linear or branched, but must not contain loops (cycles); its chemical formula is of the form CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
etymology: From German Alkan, formed as alkyl + -ane.

definition: A series of non-aromatic saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH(2n+2).
Any unsaturated aliphatic hydrocarbon.
A durable synthetic resin widely used in adhesives and paints.
etymology: From the ingredients; alkyl (alcohol) + id (acid or anhydride)

definition: A durable synthetic resin widely used in adhesives and paints.
An antineoplastic drug used to treat some forms of cancer by attaching an alkyl group to DNA.
In an allegorical manner.
example: The play ended allegorically.

definition: A quicker tempo than andante but not as fast as allegro.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian allegretto, diminutive form of allegro.

definition: Egg-thickened veloute.
Egg-thickened veloute.
A person with authority to allot or deal out or apportion.
A drug (trade name Zyloprim) used to treat gout and other conditions in which there is an excessive buildup of uric acid.
Late Jurassic carnivorous dinosaur; similar to but somewhat smaller than tyrannosaurus.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἄλλος (állos, “other, different”) + σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”).

definition: Of or pertaining to the allyl radical.
An official in a British hospital who looks after the social and material needs of the patients.
example: The almoner of a prince or bishop.
etymology: From Middle English aumener, aulmener, from Old French almosnier, from almosne (“alms”), from Latin eleemosyna. See alms, Almosen.

definition: A purgative made from the leaves of aloe.
A disposition toward being alone.
etymology: From Middle English alonnesse; equivalent to alone + -ness.

definition: Patchy baldness.
Pertaining to altitude.
example: Altitudinal variation.
etymology: From Latin altitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin altitūdō, from altus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, altitude + -al.

definition: Someone skilled in the transcription of speech (especially dictation).
etymology: From Latin āmanuēnsis (“secretary”), from ab- (“from, off (of)”) + manus (“hand”) + -ensis (“of or from (a place)”), early 17th c.

definition: Visual impairment without apparent organic pathology.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin amblyōpia. By surface analysis, ambly- + -ope + -ia.

definition: Tending to ameliorate.
Absence or suppression of normal menstrual flow.
A cylindrical spikelike inflorescence.
A radioactive transuranic metallic element; discovered by bombarding uranium with helium atoms.
etymology: From Americ(as) + -ium, by analogy with europium.

definition: Of or relating to or caused by amnesia.
example: Amnesic patients.

definition: (pregnancy) extraction by centesis of amniotic fluid from a pregnant woman (after the 15th week of pregnancy) to aid in the diagnosis of fetal abnormalities.
Pertaining to or resembling amoebae.
example: Amoebic dysentery.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: amoeb- + -ic.

definition: Inflammation of the intestines caused by Endamoeba histolytica; usually acquired by ingesting food or water contaminated with feces; characterized by severe diarrhea.
The quality of being amoral.
The reduction of the value of an asset by prorating its cost over a period of years.
Liquidate gradually.
etymology: From Middle English amortisen, from Old French amortir (via the stem amortiss-), from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”).

definition: A mineral or mineral variety belonging to the amphibole group.
etymology: From French amphibole, coined by René Just Haüy from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “ambiguous”), in reference to its many forms.

definition: A group of minerals with similar crystal structures containing a silicate chain and combinations of chiefly sodium and calcium and magnesium and iron and aluminum.
Having characteristics of both an acid and a base and capable of reacting as either.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀμφότερος (amphóteros, “each of two”), from ἄμφω (ámphō, “both”) + -τερος (-teros).

definition: A substance that acts as a base or an acid, depending on the pH of the solution into which it is introduced.
An antibiotic and antifungal agent.
Migrating from the sea to fresh water to spawn.
example: Shads and most species of salmon are anadromous.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀνάδρομος (anádromos, “fish entering a river from the sea”). By surface analysis, ana- + -dromous.

definition: A collection of excerpts from a literary work.
etymology: First attested in 1658, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλεκτα (análekta, “things chosen”), from ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + λέγω (légō, “I gather”). Compare lecture.

definition: The stage of meiosis or mitosis when chromosomes move toward opposite ends of the nuclear spindle.
etymology: 19th century: from Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “back, backward”) + φάσις (phásis, “appearance”).

definition: Using a pronoun or similar word instead of repeating a word used earlier.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀναφορά (anaphorá, “a carrying back”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + φέρω (phérō, “I carry”).

definition: Of or relating to anaplasia.
A female television reporter who coordinates a broadcast to which several correspondents contribute.
Not having or producing echoes; sound-absorbent.
example: An anechoic chamber.
etymology: From an- + echoic, from echo + -ic, from Middle English ecco, ekko, from Medieval Latin ecco, from Latin echo, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”).

definition: A chamber having very little reverberation.
Anoxia resulting from a decreased concentration of hemoglobin.
A defect in brain development resulting in small or missing brain hemispheres.
etymology: Internationalism. Learned borrowing from New Latin anencephalia. By surface analysis, an- + encephaly.

definition: Administer an anesthetic drug to.
example: The patient must be anesthetized before the operation.

definition: An abnormality involving a chromosome number that is not an exact multiple of the haploid number (one chromosome set is incomplete).
A butterfly fish of the genus Pomacanthus.
etymology: From angel + fish; so called for its wing-like pectoral fins.

definition: A heart condition marked by paroxysms of chest pain due to reduced oxygen to the heart.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin angina pectoris (1700s).

definition: Recurrent large circumscribed areas of subcutaneous edema; onset is sudden and it disappears within 24 hours; seen mainly in young women, often as an allergic reaction to food or drugs.
example: Angioedema of the throat can cause suffocation and should be treated as a medical emergency.

definition: Plants having seeds in a closed ovary.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “receptacle”) + σπέρμα (spérma, “seed”), equivalent to angio- + sperm.

definition: An admirer of England and things English.
A metric unit of length equal to one ten billionth of a meter (or 0.0001 micron); used to specify wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation.
etymology: Borrowed from Swedish ångström, named after Swedish physicist Anders Jonas Ångström.

definition: A metric unit of length equal to one ten billionth of a meter (or 0.0001 micron); used to specify wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation.
An inability to experience pleasure.
etymology: From French anhédonie (coined by Ribot, 1896), from Ancient Greek ἀν- (an-) + ἡδονή (hēdonḗ, “pleasure”).

definition: In an animated manner.
example: They talked animatedly.

definition: Of or pertaining to the doctrine of animism.
Much-branched North American herb with an odor like fennel.
A chronic form of spondylitis primarily in males and marked by impaired mobility of the spine; sometimes leads to ankylosis.
Of or at or relating to an anode.
etymology: From anode + -ic. Coined by William Whewell in 1837 in a letter to Michael Faraday.

definition: In an anomalous manner.
example: This man behaves anomalously.

definition: Personal state of isolation and anxiety resulting from a lack of social control and regulation.
etymology: From French anomie, from Ancient Greek ἀνομία (anomía, “lawlessness”), from ἄνομος (ánomos, “lawless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”). Popularized by French sociologist Émile Durkheim (1858–1917).

definition: Severe hypoxia; absence of oxygen in inspired gases or in arterial blood or in the tissues.
Anoxia resulting from defective oxygenation of the blood in the lungs.
Act in opposition to.
Of or relating to antennae.
example: Antennal senses of insects.

definition: Corresponds to the bregma when bones have ossified.
Of amnesia; affecting time immediately following trauma.
example: Anterograde amnesia is a loss of the ability to create new memories after the event that caused the amnesia.
etymology: From antero- + -grade (“direction”) from Latin gradus (“pace, step”).

definition: Loss of memory for events immediately following a trauma; sometimes in effect for events during and for a long time following the trauma.
A large entrance or reception room or area.
etymology: From ante- + room, as a calque of French antichambre or its model Italian anticamera.

definition: Relating to mankind or the period of mankind's existence.
etymology: Originated 1795–1805, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπικός (ánthrōpikós, “pertaining to human”).

definition: Human-centered.
example: Our anthropocentric view of the world.

definition: In the direction opposite to the rotation of the hands of a clock.
A drug used to treat or prevent convulsions (as in epilepsy).

definition: A drug used to treat or prevent convulsions (as in epilepsy).
Used in the treatment of cancer.

definition: Any of several drugs that control or kill neoplastic cells; used in chemotherapy to kill cancer cells; all have unpleasant side effects that may include nausea and vomiting and hair loss and suppression of bone marrow function.
(especially of vectors) parallel but oppositely directed.
example: Antiparallel vectors.

definition: A course of appetizers in an Italian meal.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian antipasto (“[food] before the meal”). Doublet of antepast.

definition: An astringent substance applied to the skin to reduce perspiration.
Relating to the antipodes or situated at opposite sides of the earth.

definition: An unstable negatively charged proton; the antiparticle of a proton.
Blood serum containing antibodies against specific antigens; provides immunity to a disease.
Defensive against enemy submarines.
example: A depth charge is an antisubmarine weapon.

definition: A word that expresses a meaning opposed to the meaning of another word, in which case the two words are antonyms of each other.

definition: (psychiatry) a relatively permanent state of worry and nervousness occurring in a variety of mental disorders, usually accompanied by compulsive behavior or attacks of panic.
A verb tense in some languages (classical Greek and Sanskrit) expressing action (especially past action) without indicating its completion or continuation.
Not recurring at regular intervals.
example: Aperiodic tiling.

definition: Apoapsis in solar orbit; the point in the orbit of a planet or comet that is at the greatest distance from the sun.
etymology: From New Latin aphēlium (whence English aphelium, now displaced) + -ion (used in the names of other apsides).

Anemia characterized by pancytopenia resulting from failure of the bone marrow; can be caused by neoplasm or by toxic exposure.
In an appealing manner.

definition: The process whereby perceived qualities of an object are related to past experience.
etymology: Borrowed from French aperception (New Latin apperceptiō, used by Gottfried Leibniz (1646–1716)).

definition: Wood of any of various apple trees of the genus Malus.
example: Applewood-smoked.

definition: Readily applicable or practical.
The act of distributing by allotting or apportioning; distribution according to a plan.
example: The apportionment of seats in the House of Representatives is based on the relative population of each state.

definition: A grammatical relation between a word and a noun phrase that follows.
example: ‘Rudolph the red-nosed reindeer’ is an example of apposition.

definition: With appreciation; in a grateful manner.
example: He accepted my offer appreciatively.

definition: Pressed close to or lying flat against something.
example: Igneous rocks … closely appressed by this force.

definition: Inform (somebody) of something.
example: The ears apprise the brain of sound.

definition: An informal British abbreviation of approval.
example: He accepted it on appro.

definition: Inability to make purposeful movements.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀπραξία (apraxía, “inaction”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + πρᾶξις (prâxis, “activity”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix). By surface analysis, a- + -praxia.

definition: An etching made by a process that makes it resemble a water color.
The middle of the 3 meninges.

definition: The middle of the 3 meninges.
A morbid fear of spiders.

definition: Any of several tall South American or Australian trees with large cones and edible seeds.
etymology: From taxonomic name Araucaria, after Spanish Arauco (“Chilean province”), from Mapudungun rag ko.

The tending of and caring for trees.
The inverse function of the secant; the angle that has a secant equal to a given number.

The territorial jurisdiction of an archbishop.

definition: The territorial jurisdiction of an archdeacon.

etymology: From Ancient Greek κοσμογονία (kosmogonía), from κόσμος (kósmos, “world”) + γόνος (gónos, “creation”). By surface analysis, cosmo- + -gony.

Small very thin pancake.

Ornamental shrub from eastern India commonly planted in the southern United States.
A risky and uncertain venture.
