Wasting time.
example: A dilatory strategy.
etymology: From Middle English dilatorie, from Old French dilatoire, from Latin dīlātōrius (“extending or putting off (time)”), from dīlātor, from differō. Not etymologically related to delay.

definition: A plea that delays the action without settling the cause of action; it can challenge the jurisdiction or claim disability of the defendant etc. (such defenses are usually raised in the defendant's answer).
Indicating or determining size and position in space.
example: The ultrasonic dimensioning measurement.

definition: A small area off of a kitchen that is used for dining.
example: The condominium lacks a proper dining room, but has a cosy dinette.

definition: A silly empty-headed person.
example: You would be a dingbat even to try it.
etymology: Unknown, US mid 19th century. The word-puzzle sense comes from the board game Dingbats, which is based on these puzzles. In the sense of a miscellaneous gadget, probably influenced by dingus or its etyma.

definition: Heartily or earnestly.
example: They fell to work dingdong.

definition: Having male and female reproductive organs in separate plants or animals.
A granular crystalline intrusive rock.
etymology: From French diorite, invented by mineralogist Alexandre Brongniart (1770-1847), derived from Ancient Greek διορίζω (diorízō, “distinguish”), from δι- plus ὁρίζω (horízō, “to limit”).

definition: A huge quadrupedal herbivore with long neck and tail; of late Jurassic in western North America.
Medical specialist whose competence has been certified by a diploma granted by an appropriate professional group.
etymology: From diploma + -ate (suffix forming nouns denoting rank or office).

definition: Having equal and opposite electric charges or magnetic poles having opposite signs and separated by a small distance.
A painting or carving (especially an altarpiece) on two panels (usually hinged like a book).
etymology: From Late Latin diptycha, plural, from Ancient Greek, neuter plural of δίπτυχος (díptukhos, “folded, doubled”), from δι- (di-) + πτυχή (ptukhḗ, “fold, layer”).

definition: Antonyms that are commonly associated (e.g., ‘wet’ and ‘dry’).
The property of a microphone or antenna of being more sensitive in one direction than in another.
example: The antenna received signals with no directivity.

definition: A type of sifter used in gardening for removing large, unwanted items form soil.
The condition of being unable to perform as a consequence of physical or mental unfitness.
example: Reading disability.

definition: Freed of a mistaken or misguided notion.
example: Some people are still not disabused of the old idea that the universe revolves around the Earth.

definition: Showing disapproval.
example: He shook his head disapprovingly.

definition: Denial of any connection with or knowledge of.
Disappointingly unsuccessful.
In a disturbing or embarrassing manner.
example: He drank some sherry, his eyes disconcertingly keen as he watched her.

definition: A longing for something better than the present situation.
A harsh mixture of sounds.
etymology: From Middle French discordance. By surface analysis, discord + -ance.

definition: An expression of lack of respect.
A person who (or that which) differentiates.
example: Keen discriminator.

definition: In a proud and domineering manner.
The act of passengers and crew getting off of a ship or aircraft.
Remove the entrails of.
Straightened out.
(medicine) any disturbance in the functioning of an organ or body part or a disturbance in the functioning of a social group.
Cause or allow (a solid substance) to flow or run out or over.
The reflex act of ejecting the contents of the stomach through the mouth.
Water in which dishes and cooking utensils are washed.
example: The dishwater drained away slowly.

definition: (informal British) sexually attractive.
example: A dishy blonde.

definition: That toward which you are inclined to feel dislike.
example: His disinclination for modesty is well known.

definition: In a disingenuous manner.
example: Disingenuously, he asked leading questions about his opponent's work.

definition: Prevent deliberately (as by making a will) from inheriting.
example: Excuses for disinheriting people, that we swear we're not making up.
etymology: From Middle English disenheriten, equivalent to dis- + inherit.

definition: Progressing melodically by intervals larger than a major second.
Serving or tending to divide or separate.
example: The words "but" and "or" are disjunctive conjunctions.
etymology: From Middle English disjunctief, disjunctyf, from Middle French disjunctif and Latin disjunctīvus (“placed in opposition”).

definition: The act of taking something apart (as a piece of machinery).
example: Russia and the United States discussed the dismantling of their nuclear weapons.

definition: Causing consternation.
Cause to be lost or disoriented.
Deprive of the possession of real estate.
etymology: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French despossesser. Equivalent to dis- + possess.

definition: Lack of proportion; imbalance among the parts of something.
example: The disproportion of the length of a building to its height.

definition: Out of proportion.
Get undressed.
example: The doctor asked the patient to disrobe before her examination.
etymology: From dis- + robe. Compare Old French desrober in the same sense.

definition: Make believe with the intent to deceive.
etymology: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English;

definition: Disagreement; especially disagreement with the government.
etymology: From Latin dissideō (“disagree”, literally “sit apart”), from dis- + sedeō (“sit”).

definition: The quality of being dissimilar.
The act of deceiving.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English dissimulacioun, from Old French dissimulation, from Latin dissimulātiō; equivalent to dissimule + -ation.

definition: The act of expanding by pressure from within.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French; cf. Latin distentio.

definition: The quality of being sharp and clear.
Unpleasantly.
A troubler who interrupts or interferes with peace and quiet; someone who causes disorder and commotion.
A drug (trade name Antabuse) used in the treatment of alcoholism; causes nausea and vomiting if alcohol is ingested.
The termination or destruction of union.
Having been divided; having the unity destroyed.
example: A league of disunited nations.

definition: A color produced by a pattern of differently colored dots that together simulate the desired color.
A color produced by a pattern of differently colored dots that together simulate the desired color.
In diverse ways.
example: The speakers treated the subject most diversely.
etymology: From Middle English diverseliche, diversliche, dyverseli, dyversely, dyversliche, dyversly, equivalent to diverse + -ly.

definition: The quality of being divisible; the capacity to be divided into parts or divided among a number of persons.
The trait of being agreeably submissive and manageable.
example: Couldn't docility from totalitarian indoctrination be a human shortcoming?
etymology: From Middle French docilité, from Latin docilitas.

definition: As a matter of doctrine.
example: He was doctrinally knowledgeable but failed to follow the basic tenets of the religion.

definition: Mentally or physically infirm with age.
example: His mother was doddering and frail.

definition: Any polyhedron having twelve plane faces.
etymology: From Ancient Greek δωδεκάεδρον (dōdekáedron). Equivalent to dodeca- + -hedron.

definition: A comic verse of irregular measure.
example: He had heard some silly doggerel that kept running through his mind.
etymology: Probably from dog + -rel (“pejorative suffix”), akin to Dog Latin, late 14th c.

definition: A comic verse of irregular measure.
example: He had heard some silly doggerel that kept running through his mind.

definition: Angle that resembles the hind leg of a dog.
etymology: The noun is derived from dog + leg, referring to the shape of the hind leg of a dog. The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: Filled with or evoking sadness.
example: The child's doleful expression.
etymology: From Middle English doleful, doolful, deolful, equivalent to dole + -ful.

definition: A prehistoric megalithic tomb typically having two large upright stones and a capstone.
etymology: Borrowed from French dolmen. Perhaps incorrectly fabricated from Breton taol maen (taol (“table”) + maen (“stone”)) (the correct compound would be *taolvaen, not **daolmaen).

definition: Of or relating to or provided in a domicile.
example: Domiciliary medical care.
etymology: From French domiciliaire, from Medieval Latin domiciliārius, from Latin domicilium (“dwelling”).

definition: The recipient of funds or other benefits.
example: John became the donee of the bone marrow donated by his brother.

definition: The main tower within the walls of a medieval castle or fortress.
etymology: A variant of dungeon remodelled on its etymon, Old French donjon.

definition: Trailing grass native to Europe now cosmopolitan in warm regions; used for lawns and pastures especially in southern United States and India.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi दूब (dūb). Doublet of durva.

definition: Small furry-tailed squirrel-like Old World rodent that becomes torpid in cold weather.
etymology: From Middle English dormowse, of uncertain origin. Possibly from a dialectal *dor-, from Old Norse dár (“benumbed”) + mous (“mouse”). More at doze, mouse.

definition: A measuring instrument for measuring doses of ionizing radiation (X-rays or radioactivity).
Mental infirmity as a consequence of old age; sometimes shown by foolish infatuations.
etymology: From Middle English dotage, from doten (“to dote”) + -age; equivalent to dote + -age.

definition: An oldster in their dotage; someone whose age has impaired their intellect.
etymology: From Middle English dotard; equivalent to dote + -ard.

definition: Having sagging folds of flesh beneath the chin or lower jaw.
Believing two contradictory ideas at the same time.
etymology: From double + think. Coined by George Orwell in 1949 as part of the Newspeak in his novel Nineteen Eighty-Four.

definition: In a doubtful manner.
example: Gerald shook his head doubtfully.
etymology: From Middle English dowtfully, doutefulli, equivalent to doubtful + -ly.

definition: A birdhouse for pigeons.
Opposed to war.
example: The Federal Reserve's statement on recent inflation was interpreted as dovish by the market.

definition: Filled with melancholy and despondency.
example: Feeling discouraged and downhearted.

definition: A change from a financially rewarding but stressful career to a less well paid but more fulfilling one.
etymology: The noun is derived from down (preposition) + shift (“slight change or movement”). The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: A downward slope or bend.
Of the front half of a stage.
Erect openly branched California shrub whose twigs are woolly when young.
Wet thoroughly.
etymology: Unknown; originally a dialectal term from southern England.

definition: Releasing someone's personal information on the Web with the intention of causing harassment.
A hymn or verse in Christian liturgy glorifying God.
A woman who cohabits with an important man.
etymology: Perhaps from Middle Dutch *doketje, diminutive of Middle Dutch docke (“a doll”), from Proto-Germanic *dokko (“something round”), related to *dukkǭ (“muscle, strength”).

definition: Half asleep.
example: A tired dozy child.

definition: Someone who is drafted and illegally refuses to serve.
Someone who is drafted into military service.
Conversion into dramatic form.
example: The play was a dramatization of a short story.

definition: The art of writing and producing plays.
Not airtight.
A strong metal bar bearing a hook to attach something to be pulled.
Untroubled by dreams.
example: A sound and dreamless sleep.

definition: Merchandise that is shoddy or inferior.
etymology: From Yiddish דרעק (drek, “dirt, crap”), from Middle High German drek, from Old High German *threc (in mūsthrec), from Proto-West Germanic *þraki, from Proto-Germanic *þrakjaz.

definition: The nest of a squirrel.
A basketball player who is dribbling the ball to advance it.
In a dry laconic manner.
A funnel-shaped device towed as a target by an airplane.
etymology: Uncertain; probably related to drag in some way.

definition: A parachute used to decelerate an object that is moving rapidly.
A small parachute that pulls the main parachute from its storage pack.
An airfield equipped with control tower and hangars as well as accommodations for passengers and cargo.
etymology: From French, from Ancient Greek δρόμος (drómos, “running”). Doublet of dromos.

definition: Swelling from excessive accumulation of watery fluid in cells, tissues, or serous cavities.
etymology: From Middle English dropesie, idropesie, from Old French idropsie, ydropisie, from Latin hydrōps, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Doublet of hydropsy and hydrops.

definition: Performed speedily and without formality.
A mound of glacial drift.
etymology: From Irish droim (“back, ridge”) + English diminutive suffix -lin (“variant of -ling”).

definition: An adherent of dualism.
example: The Manicheans were dualists.

definition: Formerly a gold coin of various European countries.
etymology: From Middle French ducat, late Old French ducat, from Old Italian ducato, from Medieval Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of dux (“duke; leader”). Doublet of duchy.

definition: Any small or minute aquatic plant of the family Lemnaceae that float on or near the surface of shallow ponds.
etymology: From duck + weed. Supposedly so-named for often being consumed by ducks and other waterfowl. Compare Middle English dokemete (“duckweed”, literally “duck-food”).

definition: Sirenian tusked mammal found from eastern Africa to Australia; the flat tail is bilobate.
A woman who is a man's sweetheart.
etymology: From Spanish Dulcinea, the name of Don Quixote's mistress in Cervantes' romance. The name in Spanish is derived from Latin dulce, from Latin dulcis.

definition: A person who is not very bright.
etymology: From Middle English dullard, dollard, equivalent to dull + -ard (pejorative agent suffix). Compare Faroese døll (“dullard, good-for-nothing, blockhead”), Norwegian Nynorsk døl (“idiot, simpleton”).

definition: Without liveliness.
example: She nodded her head dully.

definition: Stupidly or insensitively.
A small elevator used to convey food (or other goods) from one floor of a building to another.
etymology: From dumb (“unable to speak”) + waiter, originally separate words and describing the portable table's inability to relate gossip after the meal.

definition: A soft-nosed small-arms bullet that expands when it hits a target and causes a gaping wound.
etymology: From Dum Dum, a city in India where the type of bullet was developed, from Hindi दम दम (dam dam) (Bengali দমদম (domodom)), from Hindi दमदमा (damadmā, “tenaille, a raised mound or battery”).

definition: A soft-nosed small-arms bullet that expands when it hits a target and causes a gaping wound.
Leishmaniasis of the viscera.
Small common sandpiper that breeds in northern or Arctic regions and winters in southern United States or Mediterranean regions.
Apparatus that makes copies of typed, written or drawn material.
Consumer goods that are not destroyed by use.
Imprisonment (especially for a long time).
etymology: From Old French durance, from durer (“to last”).

definition: The quantity that a dustpan will hold.
Low-growing tufted deciduous shrub of northern and alpine North America having pink to coral-red flowers followed by sweet blue berries.
European erect or depressed annual weedy spurge adventive in northeastern United States.
Measuring instrument designed to measure power.
Impaired ability to learn grade-appropriate mathematics.
Painful menstruation.
Generalized feeling of distress.
A feeling of refreshing tranquility and an absence of tension or worry.
example: The easiness we feel when sleeping.

definition: An inhabitant of an eastern area; especially of the U.S.
Suitable for use as food.
etymology: From eat + -able (“able, capable”). Doublet of edible.

definition: A secret listener to private conversations.
etymology: From eavesdrop + -er (“person or thing which does”).

definition: In an eccentric or bizarre manner.
Not fake or counterfeit.
Characterized by the interdependence of living organisms in an environment.
example: An ecological disaster.

definition: A very light brown.
The outer germ layer that develops into skin and nervous tissue.
Of or relating to the ectoderm.
A person who puts finishing edges on a garment.
Make understand.
etymology: From Old French edifier (“to build, to edify”), from Latin aedificare (“build”).

definition: A specialist in the theory of education.
Entertainment that is intended to be educational.
Submerged marine plant with very long narrow leaves found in abundance along North Atlantic coasts.
Used in some classifications: essentially equivalent to Potamogetonaceae.
Inspiring a feeling of fear; strange and frightening.
Shortening of the uterine cervix and thinning of its walls as it is dilated during labor.
Power to be effective; the quality of being able to bring about an effect.
Produce.
etymology: From the participle stem of Renaissance Latin effectuare, or its source, Latin effectus (“effect”); probably after Middle French effectuer.

definition: The period of greatest prosperity or productivity.
etymology: Borrowed from French efflorescence, from Latin efflōrēscō (from ex- (“out”) + flōrēscō (“to blossom”)) + -ence. By surface analysis, effloresce + -ence.

definition: Requiring great physical effort.
Audacious (even arrogant) behavior that you have no right to.
example: We even had the effrontery to suggest that he should leave the country.
etymology: From late 17th century French effronterie, from effronté (“shameless, insolent”), from Old French esfronté, from Vulgar Latin *exfrontātus.

definition: In an effusive manner.
example: The critics praised her effusively.

definition: Eurasian rose with prickly stems and fragrant leaves and bright pink flowers followed by scarlet hips.
A conceited and self-centered person.
etymology: ego + -t- inserted to avoid hiatus, or after the analogy of dramatist, epigrammatist, etc. + -ist

definition: Characteristic of those having an inflated idea of their own importance.
Of visual imagery of almost photographic accuracy.
example: An eidetic memory.
etymology: From German eidetisch, from Ancient Greek εἰδητικός (eidētikós), from εἶδος (eîdos, “form”).

definition: (anthropology) the distinctive expression of the cognitive or intellectual character of a culture or a social group.
The ordinal number of eighty in counting order.
etymology: From earlier eighteth, from Middle English eightetithe, eiȝtetithe, eiȝtithe; equivalent to eighty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.

definition: A part of the seminal duct formed by the duct from the seminal vesicle and the vas deferens; passes through the prostate gland.
A pancreatic enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of elastin.
Diagnostic procedure consisting of recording the activity of the heart electronically with a cardiograph (and producing a cardiogram).
A graphical record of electrical activity of the brain; produced by an electroencephalograph.
The branch of physics concerned with electromagnetic phenomena.
Concerned with or producing electric current.
The rate at which energy is drawn from a source that produces a flow of electricity in a circuit; expressed in volts.

A serial arrangement of metallic elements or ions according to their electrode potentials determined under specified conditions; the order shows the tendency of one metal to reduce the ions of any other metal below it in the series.
Diagnosis of neuromuscular disorders with the use of an electromyograph.
Having a negative charge.
example: Electrons are negative.

definition: (chemistry) the tendency of an atom or radical to attract electrons in the formation of an ionic bond.
The branch of physics that deals with static electricity.
etymology: From electro- + statics. Coined by William Whewell in 1840.

definition: An alloy of gold and silver.
etymology: From Latin ēlectrum, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).

definition: Of great mass; huge and bulky.
etymology: From Latin elephantīn(us). By surface analysis, elephant + -ine.

definition: Stimulation that calls up (draws forth) a particular class of behaviors.
example: The elicitation of his testimony was not easy.

definition: Leave or strike out.
example: This vowel is usually elided before a single consonant.
etymology: From Latin ēlīdō (“to knock, dash or strike out”), from ex- (“out, away”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence e- (“assimilated form of ex-”)).

definition: Omission of a sound between two words (usually a vowel and the end of one word or the beginning of the next).
The quality of being difficult to grasp or pin down.
example: The author's elusiveness may at times be construed as evasiveness.

definition: Someone who frees others from bondage.
example: Lincoln is known as the Great Emancipator.
etymology: From Late Latin ēmancipātor, from Latin ēmancipō (“to emancipate”). By surface analysis, emancipate + -or.

definition: Deprive of strength or vigor.
example: The Senate emasculated the law.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēmasculātus (more at Etymology 1), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: Loss of power and masculinity.
example: The authoritarian regime oversaw the total emasculation of the country's judiciary.

definition: Preserve a dead body.
etymology: From Middle English enbawmen, from Middle French embaumer, from Old French embasmer. See balm.

definition: A mortician who treats corpses with preservatives.
An indentation of a shoreline larger than a cove but smaller than a gulf.
Of or relating to an embolism or embolus.
An abnormal particle (e.g. an air bubble or part of a clot) circulating in the blood.
etymology: The term was coined in 1848 by Rudolf Virchow From Latin embolus (“piston”), from Ancient Greek ἔμβολος (émbolos, “peg, stopper”).

definition: The aperture of a wind instrument into which the player blows directly.
etymology: From French embouchure, from emboucher (“to put in one’s mouth”), from en- (“in”) + bouche (“mouth”), from Latin bucca (“cheek”).

definition: Make improvements or corrections to.
example: The text was emended in the second edition.
etymology: From Middle English emenden, from Latin ēmendō (“to free from fault”), from ex- (“out”) + mendum (“fault, blemish”). Doublet of amend.

definition: The reflex act of ejecting the contents of the stomach through the mouth.
example: Syrup of ipecac almost always forces an emesis.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἔμεσις (émesis), from ἐμέω (eméō, “vomit”). Compare ἔμετος (émetos, “vomit”, noun). By surface analysis, suffixed with -esis.

definition: A basin used by bedridden patients for vomiting.
(French) a person who exercises power or influence in certain areas without holding an official position.
example: The President's wife is an eminence grise in matters of education.

definition: Compensation received by virtue of holding an office or having employment (usually in the form of wages or fees).
example: A clause in the U.S. constitution prevents sitting legislators from receiving emoluments from their own votes.
etymology: From Middle English emolument, from Old French emolument, from Latin ēmolumentum.

definition: Emotional nature or quality.
Relying on medical quackery.
example: Empiric treatment.

definition: A philosopher who subscribes to empiricism.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:empiricist.

definition: (philosophy) the doctrine that knowledge derives from experience.
Of or relating to the sky or heavens.
example: The empyrean sphere.
etymology: From Latin empȳreus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπύριος (empúrios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) (whence English pyre).

definition: An ACE inhibitor (trade name Vasotec) that blocks the formation of angiotensin in the kidney and so results in vasodilation; administered after heart attacks.
Either one of a pair of compounds (crystals or molecules) that are mirror images on each other but are not identical.
Live in or as if in a tent.
A paint consisting of pigment mixed with melted beeswax; it is fixed with heat after application.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐγκαυστικός (enkaustikós, “burning in”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”).

definition: Inflammation of the brain and spinal cord.
A concise reference book providing specific information about a subject or location.
example: The Enchiridion of Erasmus.
etymology: Either via Latin enchīridion or directly, from Ancient Greek ἐγχειρίδιον (enkheirídion, “handbook, manual”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + -ίδιον (-ídion).

definition: A formal expression of praise.
etymology: From Latin encōmium (“praise, eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion, “laudatory ode, praise”), from ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios, “of or pertaining to the victor”), from κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel, ode”).

definition: In an adorable manner.
The inner germ layer that develops into the lining of the digestive and respiratory systems.
Of or relating to or involving or practicing endodontics.
example: An endodontic specialist.

definition: The branch of dentistry dealing with diseases of the dental pulp.
A nuclease that cleaves nucleic acids at interior bonds and so produces fragments of various sizes.
The internal skeleton; bony and cartilaginous structure (especially of vertebrates).
Nutritive tissue surrounding the embryo within seeds of flowering plants.
A toxin that is confined inside the microorganisms and is released only when the microorganisms are broken down or die.

A catheter that is inserted into the trachea through the mouth or nose in order to maintain an open air passage or to deliver oxygen or to permit the suctioning of mucus or to prevent aspiration of the stomach contents.
In an enduring manner.
example: Roman culture was enduringly fertilized.

definition: Causing debilitation.
Enclose or enfold completely with or as if with a covering.
etymology: Alteration of earlier infold, from Middle English infolden, equivalent to en- + fold.

definition: In an engaging manner.
example: She played the role engagingly.

definition: Devote (oneself) fully to.
example: She seems to be completely engrossed in that book.
etymology: From Middle English engrossen, from Anglo-Norman engrosser (“to gather in large quantities, draft something in final form”); partly from the phrase en gros (“in bulk, in quantity, at wholesale”), from en- + gros;

definition: In a cryptic manner.
(law) a judicial remedy issued in order to prohibit a party from doing or continuing to do a certain activity.
In an enjoyable manner.
Photographic equipment consisting of an optical projector used to enlarge a photograph.
example: A penis enlarger.

definition: Giving spirit and vivacity.
An organic compound that contains a hydroxyl group bonded to a carbon atom which in turn is doubly bonded to another carbon atom.
A person who enrolls in (or is enrolled in) a class or course of study.
(architecture) the structure consisting of the part of a classical temple above the columns between a capital and the roof.
etymology: From Italian intavolatura, from in + tavola (“table”).

definition: Inflammation of the intestine (especially the small intestine); usually characterized by diarrhea.
Any of a group of picornaviruses that infect the gastrointestinal tract and can spread to other areas (especially the nervous system).
Cause to feel enthusiasm.
example: The novelty of the film enthused the audience.
etymology: First attested from 1827. Back-formation from enthusiasm, from Ancient Greek ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”)

definition: The ritual placing of a corpse in a grave.
Earnest or urgent request.
example: An entreaty to stop the fighting.

definition: Tie or link together.
The act of enclosing something inside something else.
With jealousy; in an envious manner.
A red fluorescent dye resulting from the action of bromine on fluorescein; used in cosmetics and as a biological stain for studying cell structures.
etymology: Borrowed from German Eosin, coined by Heinrich Caro, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in.

definition: A leukocyte readily stained with eosin.
etymology: From German eosinophil, from eosin (“rose dye, from Ancient Greek ἠώς (ēṓs, “dawn”) + -in”) + -o- + -phil.

definition: A symptom of allergic states; increased eosinophils in the blood.
etymology: Coined 1879 by American biologist Paul Ehrlich from eosin (“rosy, dawn-colored”) + -o- + -philia. By surface analysis, eosinophil + -ia.

definition: A fencing sword similar to a foil but with a heavier blade.
etymology: Borrowed from French épée, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Doublet of spatha, spathe, and spade.

definition: Jointed and nearly leafless desert shrub having reduced scalelike leaves and reddish fleshy seeds.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐφέδρα (ephédra, “sitting upon”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”).

definition: The quality or state of being momentously heroic, grand in scale or character.
A person devoted to refined sensuous enjoyment (especially good food and drink).
etymology: From Epicurus, the name of an Ancient Greek philosopher who advocated such a lifestyle.

definition: A convoluted tubule in each testis; carries sperm to vas deferens.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐπιδιδυμίς (epididumís), from ἐπί (epí, “upon, over”) + δίδυμος (dídumos, “twin; testicle”).

definition: Of or relating to the anterior walls of the abdomen.
example: Epigastric artery.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms. By surface analysis, epigastrium + -ic = epi- + gastr- + -ic = epi- + gastric.

definition: One of three arteries supplying the anterior walls of the abdomen.
Veins serving the anterior walls of the abdomen.
A flap of cartilage that covers the windpipe while swallowing.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin epiglōttis, from Ancient Greek ἐπῐγλωττῐ́ς (epĭglōttĭ́s, “valve covering the larynx”), from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “upon, over”) + γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “glottis, mouth of the windpipe”);

definition: The study of ancient inscriptions.
Of or relating to epiphytes.
example: Near-synonym: holoepiphytic.

definition: Plant that derives moisture and nutrients from the air and rain; usually grows on another plant but not parasitic on it.
Surgical incision of the perineum to enlarge the vagina and so facilitate delivery during childbirth.
etymology: From episio- + -tomy (“surgical incision”), from Ancient Greek ἐπίσιον (epísion, “pubic region”) + τέμνω (témnō, “I cut”)).

definition: Growing a crystal layer of one mineral on the crystal base of another mineral in such a manner that its crystalline orientation is the same as that of the substrate.
An official charged with the care of the horses of princes or nobles.
Stabilization by bringing into equilibrium.
Equality of distribution.
example: To my mind, the textual arguments in this case are close to equipoise.

definition: The sport of sitting on the back of a horse while controlling its movements.
Capable of being effaced.
example: A signal too loud to be erasable in a single pass through the erase head.

definition: A trivalent metallic element of the rare earth group; occurs with yttrium.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin erbium; itself from Swedish Ytterby (the name of the town where the element was discovered) + -ium. Coined by Swedish chemist and mineralogist Carl Gustaf Mosander in 1843.

definition: A type of language that has an ergative case or in which the direct object of a transitive verb has the same form as the subject of an intransitive verb.
At a previous time.
example: Her erstwhile writing.
etymology: From Middle English erste, from Old English ǣresta (“first”), from Proto-West Germanic *airist (“earliest, first”), equivalent to ere + -est.

definition: A red rash caused by hypersensitivity to a drug or disease or other allergen.
Inflammation of the esophagus; often caused by gastroesophageal reflux.
A worker skilled in giving beauty treatments (manicures and facials etc.).
Aromatic perennial of southeastern Russia.
etymology: Borrowed from French estragon. Doublet of tarragon.

definition: A naturally occurring weak estrogenic hormone secreted by the mammalian ovary; synthesized (trade name Estronol) and used to treat estrogen deficiency.
Someone who etches.
Denoting or deriving from or distinctive of the ways of living built up by a group of people.
example: Influenced by ethnic and cultural ties.
etymology: From Middle English ethnicalle, from Late Latin ethnicālis.

definition: Of or relating to ethnography.
example: Ethnographical data.

definition: An anthropologist who studies ethnology.
Anthelmintic agent used against hookworm and other nematodes.
Of or relating to the philosophical study of causation.
etymology: From etiology + -ical. By surface analysis, etio- + -logical.

definition: A tree of the genus Eucalyptus.
etymology: Shortened form of the genus name Eucalyptus.

definition: A card game similar to ecarte; each player is dealt 5 cards and the player making trump must take 3 tricks to win a hand.
etymology: Possibly from German Juckerspiel, name of an eighteenth-century Alsatian card game, itself apparently a compound of Jucker + Spiel (“game”). Likely a doublet of joker.

definition: An organism with cells characteristic of all life forms except primitive microorganisms such as bacteria; i.e. an organism with ‘good’ or membrane-bound nuclei in its cells.
etymology: Borrowed from French eucaryote; equivalent to eu- + karyon + -ote.

definition: A bivalent and trivalent metallic element of the rare earth group.
etymology: Borrowed from French europium, from Europe + -ium.

definition: A mixture of substances having a minimum melting point.
etymology: From Ancient Greek εὔτηκτος (eútēktos, “easily melted”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + τήκω (tḗkō, “to melt”). Coined as an adjective (along with the noun eutexia) by British scientist Frederick Guthrie in 1884.

definition: A person who has been evacuated from a dangerous place.
etymology: From French évacué, évacuée, from évacuer, equivalent to evacu(ate) + -ee.

definition: The four books in the New Testament (Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John) that tell the story of Christ's life and teachings.
Intentionally vague or ambiguous.
Without partiality.
example: Evenhanded justice.
etymology: From even + handed. First attested in c. 1600.

definition: North American grosbeak.
The parity of even numbers (divisible by two).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English evennesse, from Old English efennes, from Proto-West Germanic *ebnassī, from Proto-Germanic *ebnassuz, from *ebnaz (“even”) + *-assuz (“-ness”). By surface analysis, even (“flat”) + -ness.

definition: The ordinary woman.
etymology: From every + woman, modelled on earlier everyman.

definition: Give expression to.
etymology: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex- (intensive prefix)) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.

definition: A person who believes in organic evolution.
An open vessel with a handle and a spout for pouring.
etymology: From Middle English ewer, from Anglo-Norman or Old French ewer, eawer (modern French évier), from Latin aquārium, from aqua (“water”). Doublet of aquarium.

definition: With the full authority of the office.
example: The pope must speak ex cathedra for an encyclical to be infallible.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ex cathedrā (“from the (teacher's) chair”).

definition: A bet that you can pick the first and second finishers in the right order.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin exactus (literally “precise, acccurate”).

definition: The quality of being exact.
example: He demanded exactness in all details.
etymology: From French exactitude, from exact, from Latin exactus, perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due" or "measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).

definition: The quality of being exact.
example: He demanded exactness in all details.

definition: In an exaggerated manner.
A detailed inspection of your conscience (as done daily by Jesuits).
etymology: From Latin exāmen (“the tongue of a balance, examination”), for exagmen, from exigere (“to weigh accurately, to treat”): compare French examen. See exact.

definition: A bishop in one of several Eastern Orthodox Churches in North America.
Exasperate or irritate.
etymology: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin exasperātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin exasperō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out of;

definition: In an exciting manner.
example: At the time of its appearance, the movie must have seemed excitingly new, even revolutionary.

definition: Tendency to associate with only a select group.
The bodily process of discharging waste matter.
Of or relating to the process of excretion.
An organ that separates waste substances from the blood and discharges them.
Waste matter (as urine or sweat but especially feces) discharged from the body.
Of very poor quality or condition.
etymology: From Old French execrable, from Latin execrabilis.

definition: Showing by example.
etymology: From Middle English exemplificacion, exemplification, from Anglo-Norman exemplification, from Medieval Latin exemplificātiō.

definition: Sports equipment used in gymnastic exercises.
A clandestine rescue operation to bring a defector or refugee or an operative and family out of danger.
A pressing or urgent situation.
example: The health-care exigency.
etymology: From Middle French exigence, from Late Latin exigentia (“urgency”) (from exigēns + -ia), from exigere (“to demand”).

definition: Of or relating to a period of exile (especially the exile of the Jews known as the Babylonian Captivity).
Of or relating to exocrine glands or their secretions.
A gland that secretes externally through a duct.
To an exorbitant degree.
example: Prices are exorbitantly high in the capital.

definition: (rhetoric) the introductory section of an oration or discourse.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin exordium (“beginning, commencement”), from exōrdior (“to begin, commence”), from ex (“out of, from”) + ōrdior (“to begin”).

definition: Suitable for the general public.
example: Writings of an exoteric nature.
etymology: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Late Latin exōtericus + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’).

definition: In an impressively expansive manner.
example: She managed to live rather expansively on her modest income.

definition: A quality characterized by magnificence of scale or the tendency to expand.
example: The expansiveness of their extravagant life style was soon curtailed.

definition: The act of expelling a person from their native land.
example: The expatriation of wealthy farmers.
etymology: Borrowed from French expatriation, or from expatriate + -ion.

definition: A medicine promoting expectoration.
The quality of being suited to the end in view.
example: April 11 1690, John Sharp, sermon preached at White-Hall to determine concerning the expedience of actions.
etymology: From Middle English expedience, from Old French expedience, from Late Latin expedientia, from Latin expediens.

definition: Of or relating to the breathing out phase of respiration.
Capable of being explicated or accounted for.
example: Explicable behavior.
etymology: From Middle French explicable, from Latin explicabilis, from explicō (“unfold, explain”).

definition: Make plain and comprehensible.
example: My homework is to explicate a poem.

definition: A person who uses something or someone selfishly or unethically.
Tending to exploit or make use of.
Serving in or intended for exploration or discovery.
example: An exploratory operation.

definition: Suitable for export.
example: Exportable cultural achievements.

definition: A person who explains.
Of or relating to expressionism.
example: Expressionist art.

definition: With expression; in an expressive manner.
example: She gave the order to the waiter, using her hands very expressively.

definition: Deletion by an act of expunging or erasing.
With little or no preparation or forethought.
example: An extemporaneous piano recital.
etymology: Univerbation of Latin ex tempore. First attested before 1556.

definition: A nonresident doctor or medical student; connected with a hospital but not living there.
etymology: From Middle French externe or its etymon Latin externus.

definition: Regard as objective.
Surgical removal of a body part or tissue.
A criminal who extorts money from someone by threatening to expose embarrassing information about them.
Capable of being extracted.
Outside or beyond a galaxy.
example: Extragalactic nebula.

definition: (astronomy) a collection of star systems; any of the billions of systems each having many stars and nebulae and dust.
example: ‘extragalactic nebula’ is a former name for ‘galaxy’.

definition: Not regulated or sanctioned by law.
example: There were only extralegal recourses for their grievances.

definition: Carried on outside the bounds of an institution or community.
example: Extramural sports.
etymology: From Latin extramuralis, from extra (“outside”) + muralis (“of a wall”).

definition: Seemingly outside normal sensory channels.
An extravasated liquid (blood or lymph or urine); the product of extravasation.
etymology: From extravasate (“let out or force out (blood or fluid)”) + -ion; further etymology at extravasate. Attested from the 17th century.

definition: The act of releasing from a snarled or tangled condition.
(psychology) an extroverted disposition; concern with what is outside the self.
etymology: From extro- + -version. As a variant of extraversion, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's use of the (then nonstandard) spelling extrovert in her publication "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte" (1918).

definition: Form or shape by forcing through an opening.
example: Extrude steel.

definition: A substance that oozes out from plant pores.
Feel extreme happiness or elation.
etymology: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).

definition: A feeling of extreme joy.
etymology: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.

definition: A strikingly beautiful woman.
example: She was a statuesque redheaded eyeful.

definition: A tiredness of the eyes caused by prolonged close work by a person with an uncorrected vision problem.
A person who tells or invents fables.
etymology: Borrowed from French fabuliste. By surface analysis, fable + -ist, or, by surface analysis, fabula + -ist. Compare fabular.

definition: Not seriously.
example: I meant it facetiously.

definition: Not produced by natural forces.
example: Brokers created a factitious demand for stocks.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin factītius (“artificial”), alternative form of factīcius, from faciō (“to make, do”). Doublet of fetish.

definition: A servant employed to do a variety of jobs.
etymology: Ellipsis of domine fac totum, dominus fac totum /dominus factotum (“absolute ruler;

definition: A slow or gradual disappearance.
Ornament or join (fabric) by faggot stitch.
example: He fagotted the blouse for his wife.
etymology: Most likely from Italian fagotto, from Latin fascis.

definition: The stitch that ties a group of parallel threads together in fagoting.
A feeling of faintness and of being ready to swoon.
etymology: From Middle English faintnesse, feintnesse, equivalent to faint + -ness.

definition: Female falcon especially a female peregrine falcon.
A noticeable deterioration in performance or quality.
example: A falloff in quality.

definition: The opening between the false vocal folds.
Perennial herbs of the lily family having thick toxic rhizomes.
Eurasian shrub resembling the tamarisk.
Capable of being tested (verified or falsified) by experiment or observation.
example: The sentence "It will rain tomorrow" is falsifiable, while the sentence "It is what it is" is not.

definition: Very good; of the highest quality.
An overhang consisting of the fan-shaped part of the deck extending aft of the sternpost of a ship.
etymology: From fan + tail. The sense of Rhipidura-genus birds is a calque of translingual Rhipidura.

definition: Indulge in fantasies.
example: He is fantasizing when he says he plans to start his own company.

definition: A motley assortment of things.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin farrāgō (“mixed fodder; mixture, hodgepodge”), from far (“emmer (a kind of wheat), coarse meal, grits”). Doublet of farro.

definition: An installment of a printed work.
etymology: From Latin fasciculus, a diminutive of fascis (“bundle”); see also fasces. Doublet of fasciculus.

definition: A bundle of fibers (especially nerve fibers).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin fasciculus. Doublet of fascicle.

definition: In a fascinating manner.
example: Her face became fascinatingly distorted.

definition: In a fastidious and painstaking manner.
Of or relating to fatalism.
example: A fatalist person.

definition: Accumulation of hardened feces in the rectum or lower colon which the person cannot move.
Capable of producing offspring or vegetation.
etymology: From Middle French fécond, from Latin fēcundus (“fertile”), which is related to fētus and fēmina (“woman”).

definition: Enter into a league for a common purpose.
example: The republics federated to become the Soviet Union.

definition: Exhibiting an agreeably appropriate manner or style.
example: A felicitous speaker.

definition: Small terrestrial orchid of eastern North America and Europe having two nearly basal leaves and dull yellow-green racemose flowers.
A small opening covered with membrane (especially one in the bone between the middle and inner ear).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin fenestra. Existed in Middle English as fenestre, fenester, from Old English fenester (“window”).

definition: Fenestra leading into the cochlea.
The arrangement of windows in a building.
example: Foliar traits unique to Darlingtonia include the presence of transparent light-transmitting fenestrations, ...

definition: Low-lying wet land with grassy vegetation; usually is a transition zone between land and water.
etymology: From Middle English fenlond, from Old English fenland, equivalent to fen + land.

definition: Capable of being fermented.
Abounding in or covered with ferns.
example: The ferny undergrowth.
etymology: From Middle English ferny, from Old English fearniġ, equivalent to fern + -y.

definition: A metal cap or band placed on a wooden pole to prevent splitting.
etymology: From Middle English verel, virel, virole (“ferrule;

definition: Make fertile or productive.
example: The course fertilized her imagination.

definition: Characterized by intense emotion.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fervidus, from ferveō. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + id.

definition: A curtain of fabric draped and bound at intervals to form graceful curves.
Make a fetish of.
example: Our society has fetishized personal wealth.

definition: Bound by chains fastened around the ankles.
Someone who tells lies.
A trivial act of lying or being deliberately unclear.
A very slender natural or synthetic fiber.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fibrilla, diminutive of Latin fibra. Doublet of fibrilla. Compare fibre.

definition: A nervous belligerent little mongrel dog.
Unfaithfulness by virtue of being unreliable or treacherous.
etymology: From Middle English fikelnesse, equivalent to fickle + -ness.

definition: Densely tufted perennial chickweed of north temperate zone.
Of Eurasia and Greenland and North America.
European plant with minute axillary blue flowers on long stalks; widely naturalized in America.
A disease caused by nematodes in the blood or tissues of the body causing blockage of lymphatic vessels.
Make off with belongings of others.
example: Hey, someone filched my wallet!
etymology: From Middle English filchen (“to pilfer, steal”).

definition: Thin in diameter; resembling a thread.
example: Tiger beetles have filiform antennae.

definition: Anything that tends to arouse.
example: His approval was an added fillip.
etymology: From Middle English filippen, philippe (“to flick or snap a finger from against the thumb”); further origin uncertain, but probably imitative. See flip.

definition: The product of filtration; a gas or liquid that has been passed through a filter.
etymology: From the substantivation of New Latin filtrātus (“filtered”) past perfect participle of filtrō (“to filter”). Equivalent to filter (the verb) + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

definition: Achieve something by means of trickery or devious methods.
example: Finagle a day off work.
etymology: Americanism from the 1920s, perhaps combining an alteration of fainaigue (“to renege”) with the suffix + -le (“frequentative”), possibly influenced by inveigle; compare haggle.

definition: The act of finalizing.
A mixture of finely chopped fresh herbs.
example: An omelet flavored with fines herbes.

definition: A young or small fish.
etymology: From Middle English fyngyrlynge, equivalent to finger + -ling, from having the size of a human finger.

definition: A long narrow inlet of the sea between steep cliffs; common in Norway.
A performer who pretends to swallow fire.
Any strong spirits (such as strong whisky or rum).
etymology: A calque of a Native American language term, probably Ojibwe ishkodewaaboo (“alcohol”), from ishkodew- (“fire”) + -aaboo (“liquid”, glossed in older works as “water”).

definition: A British unit of capacity equal to 9 imperial gallons.
etymology: From Middle Dutch *vierdekijn, diminutive of vierde (“fourth”), from vier (“four”); equivalent to fourth + -kin.

definition: A sharp barbed hook for catching fish.
etymology: From Middle English fisch-hook, from Old English *fischōc (“fishhook”), equivalent to fish + hook. Cognate with Dutch vishaak (“fishhook”).

definition: A freshwater pond with fish.
etymology: From Middle English fishpond; equivalent to fish + pond.

definition: Capable of undergoing nuclear fission.
example: A fissionable nucleus.

definition: In a fitful manner.
example: He slept fitfully.

definition: (of conifers) having five needles.
A compound (such as ethanol or formaldehyde) that fixes tissues and cells for microscopic study.
In a fixed manner.
example: He stared at me fixedly.
etymology: From fixed (“not changing; not able to be changed, staying the same”) + -ly (suffix forming adverbs from adjectives).

definition: Having or resembling a lash or whip (as does a flagellum).
etymology: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin flagellātus perfect passive participle of flagellō (“to whip, flog”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Having or resembling a lash or whip (as does a flagellum).
Any cell or one-celled organism equipped with a flagellum.
In a fancy colorful manner.
example: He dresses rather flamboyantly.

definition: Purplish-red table grape.
A lamp for providing momentary light to take a photograph.
An unintended electric discharge (as over or around an insulator).
A believer in a conspiracy theory, especially that the earth is flat.
Sweet lean whitish flesh of any of numerous thin-bodied fish; usually served as thin fillets.
A policeman who patrols a given region.
etymology: From flat + foot. Piecewise doublet of platypus.

definition: A person who uses flattery.
etymology: From Middle English flaterere, equivalent to flatter + -er.

definition: A closely cropped haircut; usually for men or boys.
etymology: From flat + top. Sense of “aircraft carrier” attributed to the message, “Scratch one flattop,” radioed during the Battle of the Coral Sea by LCDR Robert E.

definition: Generating excessive gas in the alimentary canal.
example: Sorry, I'm a bit flatulent at the moment - just eaten some curry.

definition: Someone who plays the flute.
Full of flavor.
Full of flavor.
Of hair color; pale yellowish to yellowish brown.
example: Flaxen locks.
etymology: From Middle English flaxen, flexon, flexin, from Old English fleaxen (“of flax; flaxen”), equivalent to flax + -en (“made of”). Compare Dutch vlassen.

definition: A run-down hotel.
example: He's become a real fleabag recently. Time for a bath!

definition: Feed, care for, and rear young birds for flight.
(of fabrics) having soft nap produced by brushing.
example: A fleecy lining.

definition: Someone who flees from an uncongenial situation.
etymology: Possibly from a Scandinavian source, compare Norwegian bokmål flire (“to giggle”), Jutish Danish flire.

definition: Marked by the appetites and passions of the body.
example: Fleshly desire.
etymology: From Middle English fleschly, from Old English flǣsċlīċ; equivalent to flesh + -ly.

definition: Having feathers.
example: Arrows flighted argent.

definition: Deceive somebody.
etymology: Ultimately a sound-symbolic reduplication, 1538 as noun, 1660 as verb. Perhaps from a dialectal word or North Germanic/Scandinavian; compare Old Norse flim (“lampoon, mockery”).

definition: Move back and forth very rapidly.
etymology: From Middle English flytteren, frequentative form of flitten, flytten, flütten, possibly from Old Norse flytja (“to carry about, convey”), equivalent to flit + -er (frequentative suffix).

definition: A small loosely aggregated mass of flocculent material suspended in or precipitated from a liquid.
etymology: From Latin floccus (“tuft of wool”), or from French floc (“floc”), from the same Latin source.

definition: The process of flocculating; forming woolly cloudlike aggregations.
A torturer who flogs or scourges (especially an official whose duty is to whip offenders).
etymology: From flog + -er. Compare Low German flogger (“a flail”).

definition: A prostitute who attracts customers by walking the streets.
A diminutive flower (especially one that is part of a composite flower).
etymology: From Old French florete, diminutive of flor (“flower”). Doublet of fleuret and floweret.

definition: The cultivation of flowering plants.
Like down or as soft as down.
A strip of pleated material used as a decoration or a trim.
etymology: Probably of North Germanic origin, from Norwegian flunsa (“hurry”), perhaps ultimately imitative. Or, perhaps formed on the pattern of pounce, bounce.

definition: Resembling flour in fine powdery texture.
example: A floury clay.

definition: A bed in which flowers are growing.
Common perennial United States spurge having showy white petallike bracts.
A container in which plants are cultivated.
Exhibit or undergo fluorescence.
A halocarbon in which some hydrogen atoms have been replaced by fluorine; used in refrigerators and aerosols.
A plastic made with fluorocarbon.
Examination of body structures using a fluoroscope.
A pathological condition resulting from an excessive intake of fluorine (usually from drinking water).
An antimetabolite used to treat certain cancers.
Be flustered; behave in a confused manner.
example: He seemed to fluster when speaking in front of many people.
etymology: The verb is probably from Middle English *flostren (implied in flostring, flostrynge (“agitation; blustering”)) from a Scandinavian (North Germanic) language; compare Icelandic flaustra (“to bustle”), flaustr (“a bustle;

definition: A groove or furrow in cloth etc. (particularly a shallow concave groove on the shaft of a column).
Guided by whim and fancy.
Tropical fish with huge fanlike pectoral fins for underwater gliding; unrelated to searobins.
A blank leaf in the front or back of a book.
A flight at a low altitude (usually of military aircraft) over spectators on the ground.
The geographic route along which birds customarily migrate.
Hammer into thin flat foils.
example: Foliate metal.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin foliātus (“having leaves, leafy, leaved”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), a participial adjective derived from folium (“leaf;

definition: Ornamented with foliage or foils.
example: Foliate tracery.

definition: (botany) the process of forming leaves.
example: They show that curved inclusion trails may form even with no coupling, as the porphyroblast overgrows foliation that is deflected around it.
etymology: From French foliation, from Latin folium (“leaf”).

definition: A song that is traditionally sung by the common people of a region and forms part of their culture.
Inflammation of a hair follicle.
Any membranous gap between the bones of the cranium in an infant or fetus.
etymology: Borrowed from French fontanelle, from Old French fontenelle, a diminutive of fontaine (“fountain, spring”) + -elle, from Late Latin fontāna, from Latin fontānus, from font- + -ānus.

definition: Foolish or senseless behavior.
etymology: From Middle English foleri, ffollery, equivalent to fool + -ery.

definition: A low seat or a stool to rest the feet of a seated person.
Affecting extreme elegance in dress and manner.
Physical energy or intensity.
example: He hit with all the force he could muster.

definition: The act of crossing a stream or river by wading or in a car or on a horse.
A person from whom you are descended.
The deck between the bridge and the forecastle.
The forelimb of a quadruped.
The front limb (or the homologous structure in other animals, such as a flipper or wing).
A lock of hair growing (or falling) over the forehead.
etymology: From Middle English *forelock, *forelok, from Old English forelocc, equivalent to fore- + lock.

definition: The mast nearest the bow in vessels with two or more masts.
The time period between dawn and noon.
etymology: From Middle English forenone, equivalent to fore- + noon.

definition: The act of preventing something by anticipating and disposing of it effectively.
The basic unit of money in Hungary.
etymology: From Hungarian forint, from Italian fiorino (“florin, the former currency of Tuscany”). Doublet of florin.

definition: In a forlorn manner.
example: A single chicken was scratching forlornly in the yard.

definition: Make formal or official.
example: We formalized the appointment and gave him a title.

definition: In a formidable manner.
example: The constant risk that attends the exchanges of human beings formidably armed.

definition: Have sex without being married.
etymology: First attested in 1552; borrowed from Latin fornicātus, perfect active participle of fornicor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fornix (“arch, vault; brothel”).

definition: Any of various early blooming oleaceous shrubs of the genus Forsythia; native to eastern Asia and southern Europe but widely cultivated for their branches of bright yellow bell-shaped flowers.
etymology: From New Latin, named in honor of Scottish horticulturist William Forsyth, who brought the shrub over from China. Forsyth's own name is from Irish Fearsithe, meaning "man of peace."

definition: Directly and without evasion; not roundabout.
example: Spoke forthright (or forthrightly) and to the point.

definition: (chiefly a direction or description in music) very loud and strong.
Partly mineralized copal dug from the ground.
Disgusting wickedness and immorality.
example: He understood the foulness of sin.
etymology: From Middle English foulnesse, foulnes, from Old English fūlnes (“foulness”), equivalent to foul + -ness. Compare Dutch vuilnis (“rubbish; garbage; trash”).

definition: (of conifers) having four needles.
Medium-sized glossy-coated hounds developed for hunting foxes.
Grasses of the genera Alopecurus and Setaria having dense silky or bristly brushlike flowering spikes.
example: Look at the foxtails growing along the road.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fox-tail. By surface analysis, fox + tail.

definition: Barley grown for its highly ornamental flower heads with delicate long silky awns; North America and northeastern Asia.
Ground pine thickly covered with bristly leaves; widely distributed in barren sandy or peaty moist coastal regions of eastern and southeastern United States.
