definition: Directed toward heaven or the sky.
example: The soul in its heavenward flight.
etymology: From Middle English hevenward, heveneward, hefneward, equivalent to heaven + -ward.

definition: Having a short and solid form or stature.
example: He was tall and heavyset.

definition: A respondent who avoids giving a clear direct answer.
etymology: From Middle English hegger, equivalent to hedge + -er.

definition: Extreme nervousness.
example: I don't mind worms, but spiders give me the heebie-jeebies.

definition: Any plant of the genus Helianthus having large flower heads with dark disk florets and showy yellow rays.
etymology: From the genus name. Compare helio- (“sun”), antho- (“flower”).

definition: A tuba that coils over the shoulder of the musician.
etymology: Probably from helic- + -on (“augmentative suffix”), from Ancient Greek ἕλῐξ (hélĭx) + -on, after bombardon.

definition: The region inside the heliopause containing the sun and solar system.
Green chalcedony with red spots that resemble blood.
etymology: PIE word *sóh₂wl̥ The noun is borrowed from French héliotrope, from Latin hēliotropium (“plant which turns to face the sun;

definition: Perennial herbs of the lily family having thick toxic rhizomes.
etymology: From Middle English ellebore, from Old French ellebre, elebore, from Medieval Latin eleborus, via Latin from Ancient Greek ἑλλέβορος (helléboros), possibly from ἄλκη (álkē, “elk [moose]”) βιβρώσκω (bibrṓskō, “to eat”).

definition: A very evil man.
etymology: From Middle English helle hound; equivalent to hell + hound.

definition: Worm that is parasitic on the intestines of vertebrates especially roundworms and tapeworms and flukes.
A helpful partner.
etymology: A folk-etymological alteration of helpmeet, by reanalysis as help + mate.

definition: Benign angioma consisting of a mass of blood vessels; some appear as birthmarks.
A soft red birthmark.
The ratio of the volume occupied by packed red blood cells to the volume of the whole blood as measured by a hematocrit.
etymology: From hemato- (“blood”) + Ancient Greek κριτής (kritḗs, “judge, umpire”), literally “to separate blood”, coined by Swedish physiologist Magnus Blix in 1891.

definition: A doctor who specializes in diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs.
The presence of blood in the urine; often a symptom of urinary tract disease.
Paralysis of one side of the body.
example: I call the series Dubliners to betray the soul of that hemiplegia or paralysis which many consider a city.
etymology: From New Latin hemiplegia, from Ancient Greek ἡμιπλήξ (hēmiplḗx), also ἡμιπληγής (hēmiplēgḗs, “stricken on one side”), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”). By surface analysis, hemi- + -plegia.

definition: The line formed by the lower edge of a skirt or coat.
example: Above-knee hemline.

definition: Pathology in which iron accumulates in the tissues; characterized by bronzed skin and enlarged liver and diabetes mellitus and abnormalities of the pancreas and the joints.
etymology: From hemo- (“blood”) + chromat- (“color”) + -osis (“disease”), from the changing color of blood affected by the disorder.

definition: An acute infectious disease characterized by pneumonia and blood infection.
From this time forth; from now on.
example: Henceforth she will be known as Mrs. Smith.
etymology: From Middle English hennes forward, equivalent to hence + forward. Compare Middle English hens-forthward, hennes forthward (“henceforward”).

definition: Harassed by persistent nagging.
Common tanager of southwestern United States and Mexico.
Any of several plants of the genus Hepatica having three-lobed leaves and white or pinkish flowers in early spring; of moist and mossy subalpine woodland areas of north temperate regions.
Succulent herbaceous vegetation of pastureland.
etymology: From Middle English herbage, from Old French erbage, from Early Medieval Latin herbāticum, from Latin herba (“grass”). By surface analysis, herb + -age.

definition: Of or relating to monoclinous plants.
A zoologist who studies reptiles and amphibians.
etymology: From herpeto- (From Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón, “creeping animal, reptile, especially a snake”)) + -logist.

definition: The branch of zoology concerned with reptiles and amphibians.
etymology: Derived from French herpétologie, from Ancient Greek ἑρπετόν (herpetón, “reptile”) + -logie (suffix indicating a field of study or work), equivalent to herpet- + -logy.

definition: A feeling of diffidence and indecision about doing something.
example: His hesitance was caused by bad past experiences.

definition: Of or relating to the beat produced by heterodyning two oscillations.
An oscillator whose output heterodynes with the incoming radio signal to produce sum and difference tones.
A radio receiver that combines a locally generated frequency with the carrier frequency to produce a supersonic signal that is demodulated and amplified.
Consisting of elements that are not of the same kind or nature.
example: The population of the United States is vast and heterogeneous.

definition: Not corresponding in structure or evolutionary origin.
etymology: By surface analysis, heterologue + -ous, or, by surface analysis, heterology + -ous.

definition: Requiring organic compounds of carbon and nitrogen for nourishment.
example: Most animals are heterotrophic.

definition: The 8th letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
A person who hews.
A regular polygon formed by extending each of the sides of a regular hexagon to form two equilateral triangles.
A verse line having six metrical feet.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἑξάμετρος (hexámetros). Equivalent to hexa- + meter. Piecewise doublet of sexameter.

definition: (usually used colloquially) causing or accompanied by misfortune.
Stubbornly conservative and narrow-minded.
example: 1644-1646, Francis Quarles, Boanerges and Barnabas hath my purse been hidebound to my hungry brother?
etymology: From hide (“animal skin”, noun) + bound (“tied”, adjective).

definition: A person who holds a high position in a hierarchy.
etymology: From Medieval Latin hierarcha, from Ancient Greek ἱεράρχης (hierárkhēs) Derived from ἱερός (hierós, “holy”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler”, “leader”). ἱερός from Proto-Hellenic *iherós, from Proto-Indo-European *ish₁ros.

definition: Associated with the priesthood or priests.
example: Hieratic gestures.
etymology: From Latin hieraticus, from Ancient Greek ἱερατικός (hieratikós), from ἱερατεία (hierateía, “priesthood”), from ἱερατεύω (hierateúō, “be a priest”), from ἱερεύς (hiereús, “priest”), from ἱερός (hierós, “sacred”).

definition: A cursive form of Egyptian hieroglyphics; used especially by the priests.
Writing that resembles hieroglyphics (usually by being illegible).
example: Hieroglyphs were discovered on the wall inside the temple.

definition: Having a higher than normal ceiling.
Belonging to the peerage.
A chair for feeding a very young child; has four long legs and a footrest and a detachable tray.
Retreat at full speed.
example: He hightailed it toward town.
etymology: From high + tail; refers to the behavior of fleeing animals, such as deer, that raise their tail when running away.

definition: Flee; take to one's heels; cut and run.
example: He started to hightail it out of there, but I stopped him at the door.

definition: Of or relating to or located near a hilum.
The posterior portion of the brain including cerebellum and brainstem.
Something immaterial that interferes with or delays action or progress.
A person responsible for hiring workers.
Excessive hairiness.
Condition in which the cells of one tissue can survive in the presence of cells of another tissue.
example: A successful graft or transplant requires a high degree of histocompatibility.

definition: A throaty harshness.
example: The hoarseness of her voice was caused by years of smoking.
etymology: From Middle English hosnesse, from Old English hāsnes; equivalent to hoarse + -ness.

definition: Rub elbows with.
example: He hobnobs with the best of society.
etymology: From hob and nob, hob or nob (“a phrase spoken when making a toast, possibly meaning ‘give and take’;

definition: (of a ship) so weakened as to sag at each end.
A British unit of capacity for alcoholic beverages.
The common people generally.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek οἱ πολλοί (hoi polloí, “the many”).

definition: A thick sweet and pungent Chinese condiment.
etymology: Partial calque from Cantonese 海鮮醬／海鲜酱 (hoi2 sin1 zoeng3, literally “seafood sauce, sauce for seafood”).

definition: A capacious bag or basket.
The theory that the parts of any whole cannot exist and cannot be understood except in their relation to the whole.
example: Holism holds that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
etymology: From hol- (“whole, entire, total”) + -ism. Coined in 1926 by Jan Smuts.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Althaea; similar to but having smaller flowers than genus Alcea.
etymology: From Middle English holihocke, holyhokke, holihoc, from holi (“holy”) + hocke, hokke, hoc (“mallow”) (from Old English hoc (“marsh mallow”).

definition: Someone who builds houses as a business.
Someone who settles lawfully on government land with the intent to acquire title to it.
Hulled corn with the bran and germ removed.
Coarsely ground hulled corn boiled as a breakfast dish in the southern United States.
Of or relating to the practice of homeopathy.
A method of treating disease with small amounts of remedies that, in large amounts in healthy people, produce symptoms similar to those being treated.
All similarly.
example: The students at this college are homogeneously middle-class.

definition: Cause to become equal or homogeneous as by mixing.
example: Homogenize the main ingredients.

definition: Two words are homonyms if they are pronounced and spelled the same way but have different meanings.
etymology: From Latin homōnymum, from Ancient Greek ὁμώνυμον (homṓnumon), nominalized from the neuter of ὁμώνῠμος (homṓnŭmos, “homonymous”). By surface analysis, hom- + -onym.

definition: Two words are homophones if they are pronounced the same way but differ in meaning or spelling or both (e.g. bare and bear).
etymology: From French homophone; equivalent to homo- (“same”) + -phone (“sound”).

definition: A degree conferred to honor the recipient.
etymology: From Latin honoris causa (“for the sake of the honor”).

definition: Small North American duck with a high circular crest on the male's head.
Influence by slyness.
etymology: The verb is derived from hood (“head covering attached to a larger garment such as a jacket or cloak”) + wink (“to close one’s eyes”). (< C16 'to blindfold'). The noun is derived from the verb.

definition: Senseless talk.
example: I heard his speech. It sounded like a whole lot of hooey to me.
etymology: Possibly related to phooey, possibly a euphemism for horseshit, or possibly from Ukrainian or Russian хуй (xuj). Compare hooie (interjection) and German hui.

definition: Dancing in which the steps are more important than gestures or postures.
Any of several trees resembling hornbeams with fruiting clusters resembling hops.
etymology: From the resemblance of the fruit to hops. See hornbeam.

definition: Full of hope.
Spanish traditional beverage, made of ground almonds, sesame seeds, rice, barley, tigernuts (chufas), or melon seeds.
Any of several trees or shrubs of the genus Carpinus.
etymology: From Late Middle English hornbeme, hernbem, hernebem (“European hornbeam (Carpinus betulus)”), from horn (“antler or horn of an animal; etc.”) + bem (“tree;

definition: Bird of tropical Africa and Asia having a very large bill surmounted by a bony protuberance; related to kingfishers.
A green to black mineral of the amphibole group; consists of silicates of calcium and sodium and magnesium and iron.
etymology: From German Hornblende, from Horn (“horn”) + Blende (see blende).

definition: The art of designing and making clocks.
etymology: From Latin horologia, from horo- + -logia, equivalent to Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “period of time, hour”) + -λογία (-logía, “-ology: study or proper knowledge of”). Equivalent to horo- + -ology.

definition: An early term for an automobile.
example: When automobiles first replaced horse-drawn carriages they were called horseless carriages.
etymology: Early term for an automobile, at the time it was common that carriages were pulled by animals, typically horses, but the automobiles were not.

definition: The flesh of horses as food.

Perennial rushlike flowerless herbs with jointed hollow stems and narrow toothlike leaves that spread by creeping rhizomes; tend to become weedy; common in Northern Hemisphere; some in Africa and South America.
etymology: From Middle English horsetaile, horstaile, equivalent to horse + tail.

definition: Sole surviving family of the Equisetales: fern allies.
Any of several lichens of the genus Alectoria having a thallus consisting of filaments resembling hair.
Milkweed of southwestern United States and Mexico; poisonous to livestock.
A woman skilled in equitation.
Deciduous shrub bearing roundheaded flower clusters opening green and aging to pink or blue.
etymology: From the genus name, New Latin Hortensia, from hortēnsius (“of the garden”), from hortēnsis.

definition: A flexible pipe for conveying a liquid or gas.
A tradesman who sells hosiery and (in England) knitwear.
example: William Blake's father was a hosier.
etymology: From Middle English hosiere; equivalent to hose + -ier.

definition: Admit into a hospital.
example: Mother had to be hospitalized because her blood pressure was too high.
etymology: From hospital + -ize. Piecewise doublet of hotelize.

definition: A hotel providing overnight lodging for travelers.
example: The hostelry trade.
etymology: From Middle English hostelerie, from Middle French hostellerie, from Old French hostelerie, ostelerie; by surface analysis, hostel + -ry.

definition: A journal bearing (as of a railroad car) that has overheated.
Quickly aroused to anger.
example: A hotheaded commander.

definition: A portable electric appliance for heating or cooking or keeping food warm.
(of pets) trained to urinate and defecate outside or in a special place.
example: Housebroken pets.

definition: Common fly that frequents human habitations and spreads many diseases.
etymology: From house + fly. Cognate with Dutch huisvlieg (“housefly”), Danish husflue (“housefly”), Swedish husfluga (“housefly”), Faroese húsfluga (“housefly”).

definition: Teacher in charge of a school boardinghouse.
A sandal with flat heels and an upper of woven leather straps.
etymology: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish huarache, guarache, from Purepecha kwarachi (“sandal”).

definition: Cap that fits over the hub of a wheel.
The quality of compassion or consideration for others (people or animals).
etymology: From humane + -ness. Piecewise doublet of humanness.

definition: The act of making more human.
Suggesting human characteristics for animals or inanimate things.
The quality of being human.
etymology: From human + -ness. Piecewise doublet of humaneness.

definition: Someone of remarkable excellence.
example: A humdinger of a secretary.
etymology: US origin, perhaps a blend of hummer (“something that moves fast”) + dinger (“something outstanding”). First attested in a newspaper article in the Daily Enterprise of June 4, 1883, at Livingston, Montana.

definition: The act of indulging or gratifying a desire.
Lacking humor.
Characteristic of or suffering from kyphosis, an abnormality of the vertebral column.
An extreme bellicose nationalist.
By a factor of one hundred.
example: Their money increased a hundredfold.
etymology: From Middle English hundredfold. Equivalent to hundred + -fold.

definition: An unemployed person who participates in a hunger march.
(baseball) the person who does the pitching.
A disorderly outburst or tumult.
An enzyme (trade name Hyazyme) that splits hyaluronic acid and so lowers its viscosity and increases the permeability of connective tissue and the absorption of fluids.
Breed animals or plants using parents of different races and varieties.
(genetics) the act of mixing different species or varieties of animals or plants and thus to produce hybrids.
A diuretic drug (trade name Microzide, Esidrix, and HydroDIURIL) used in the treatment of hypertension.
Electricity produced by water power.
Colonial coelenterates having the polyp phase dominant.
A geologist skilled in hydrology.
Undergo hydrolysis; decompose by reacting with water.
A measuring instrument for determining the specific gravity of a liquid or solid.
A narcotic analgesic (trade name Dilaudid) used to treat moderate to severe pain.
The property of being water-repellent; tending to repel and not absorb water.
An airplane that can land on or take off from water.
example: The designer of marine aircraft demonstrated his newest hydroplane.

definition: Racing in high-speed motor boats.
Containing combined water (especially water of crystallization as in a hydrate).
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὑδροῦς (hudroûs), from the combining form of ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + -οῦς (-oûs, “-ous, -ful”). Equivalent to hydro- + -ous. Doublet of Otranto and Hydruntum.

definition: Anti-inflammatory drug (trade name Plaquenil) used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and malaria and lupus erythematosus.
(ethnic slur) offensive term for a Jew.
The presence of abnormally high levels of calcium in the blood; usually the result of excessive bone resorption in hyperparathyroidism or Paget's disease.
The presence of an abnormal amount of cholesterol in the cells and plasma of the blood; associated with the risk of atherosclerosis.
Inclined to judge too severely.
example: Hypercritical of colloquial speech.

definition: Severe and excessive vomiting.
Extremely fine or thin, as in a spectral line split into two or more components.
example: Hyperfine structure.

definition: Excessive and profuse perspiration.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, from New Latin, from hyper- + hidrosis.

definition: Higher than normal levels of potassium in the circulating blood; associated with kidney failure or sometimes with the use of diuretic drugs.
Presence of excess lipids in the blood.
A multimedia system in which related items of information are connected and can be presented together.
etymology: From hyper- + media, coined by American information technologist, philosopher, and sociologist Ted Nelson in 1965.

definition: A multimedia system in which related items of information are connected and can be presented together.
Excessive secretion of parathyroid hormone resulting in abnormally high levels of calcium in the blood; can affect many systems of the body (especially causing bone resorption and osteoporosis).
(of living tissue) in a state of abnormally high tension.
example: Hypertonic muscle tissue.

definition: Any solution with a higher salt concentration than normal body cells so that the water is drawn out of the cells by osmosis.
example: A hypertonic solution has higher osmotic pressure than another solution.

definition: Divide or connect with a hyphen.
example: Hyphenate these words and names.

definition: Sleep inducing.
By means of hypnotism.
Chronic and abnormal anxiety about imaginary symptoms and ailments.
example: Near-synonyms: hypochondriasis, valetudinarianism.
etymology: From New Latin hypochondria (the morbid condition so called, supposed to have its seat in the upper part of the abdomen), from hypochondrium (see English hypochondrium for more).

definition: Abnormally low blood sugar usually resulting from excessive insulin or a poor diet.
Abnormally low level of potassium in the circulating blood leading to weakness and heart abnormalities; associated with adrenal tumors or starvation or taking diuretics.
An achondroplastic dwarf whose small size is the result of a genetic defect; body parts and mental and sexual development are normal.
The suppression of a gene by the effect of an unrelated gene.
etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin hypostasis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόστασις (hupóstasis, “sediment, foundation; substance, existence, essence”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under”) + στάσις (stásis, “standing”).

definition: (of muscular tissue) the state of being hypotonic.
etymology: From New Latin hypotonia, from hypo- + Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos) + -ia. By surface analysis, hypo- + -tonia.

definition: A European mint with aromatic and pungent leaves used in perfumery and as a seasoning in cookery; often cultivated as a remedy for bruises; yields hyssop oil.
etymology: Via Latin hȳsōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), of Semitic origin.

definition: Used chiefly in liqueurs.
Induced by a physician's words or therapy (used especially of a complication resulting from treatment).
A substance used to melt ice; it can take a form of liquid or solid crystals.
example: Darling, the driveway is covered in ice again, I think we should buy an ice melter before someone slips and breaks a leg.

definition: Locked in by ice.
example: Icebound harbors.

definition: A steep part of a glacier resembling a frozen waterfall.
etymology: From ice + fall, modelled after waterfall.

definition: The branch of zoology that studies fishes.
Any of several congenital diseases in which the skin is dry and scaly like a fish.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin ichthyōsis. By surface analysis, ichthyo- + -osis. First attested in 1815.

definition: Of or relating to an icosahedron.
Any polyhedron having twenty plane faces.
etymology: From Ancient Greek εἰκοσάεδρον (eikosáedron), from εἴκοσι (eíkosi, “twenty”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “face of a geometrical solid”). Equivalent to icosa- + -hedron.

definition: Yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes caused by an accumulation of bile pigment (bilirubin) in the blood; can be a symptom of gallstones or liver infection or anemia.
etymology: From the Latin icterus, from the Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros, “jaundice”).

definition: Unchanged in value following multiplication by itself.
example: This matrix is idempotent.
etymology: From Latin roots idem (“same”) + potent (“having power”), thus “having the same power”. Coined in 1870 by American mathematician Benjamin Peirce in the context of algebra, later generalized to computer science.

definition: In an identifiable manner.
example: They were identifiably different.

definition: A behavioral attribute that is distinctive and peculiar to an individual.
etymology: First attested in 1604, in modern sense since 1665, from Ancient Greek ἰδιοσυγκρασία (idiosunkrasía, “one’s own temperament”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one’s own”) + σύν (sún, “together”) + κρᾶσις (krâsis, “temperament”).

definition: In an idiotic manner.
example: What arouses the indignation of the honest satirist is not the fact that people in positions of power or influence behave idiotically.

definition: Love unquestioningly and uncritically or to excess; venerate as an idol.
example: Many teenagers idolized the Beatles.

definition: Regarded with deep or rapturous love (especially as if for a god).
example: An idolized wife.

definition: In a dishonorable manner or to a dishonorable degree.
etymology: From ignominious + -ly (suffix forming adverbs from nouns).

definition: Surgical procedure that creates an opening from the ileum through the abdominal wall to function as an anus; performed in cases of cancer of the colon or ulcerative colitis.
The part of the small intestine between the jejunum and the cecum.
etymology: Via Medieval Latin from Latin ilia.

definition: In a manner disapproved or not allowed by custom.
example: He acted illegitimately when he increased the rent fourfold.

definition: Invalid or incorrect reasoning.
In an illogical manner.
example: She acted illogically under the pressure.

definition: A weakly magnetic black mineral found in metamorphic and plutonic rocks; an iron titanium oxide in crystalline form; a source of titanium.
etymology: Named after Ilmen Mountains in Russia + -ite in 1827.

definition: Having a mental age of three to seven years.
An intricate and confusing interpersonal or political situation.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian imbroglio (“tangle, entanglement, muddle”) (im-, alternative form of in- (prefix forming verbs denoting derivation) + broglio (“confusion; intrigue, fraud, rigging, stuffing”);

definition: An organic base C3H4N2; a histamine inhibitor.
A tricyclic antidepressant (trade names Imavate and Tofranil) used to treat clinical depression.
The act of limiting movement or making incapable of movement.
example: The storm caused complete immobilization of the rescue team.

definition: Beyond reasonable limits.
example: Immoderate laughter.
etymology: From Middle English inmoderat, immoderate, from Latin immoderātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

definition: Having been rendered unsusceptible to a disease.
Any substance or organism that provokes an immune response (produces immunity) when introduced into the body.
Possessing the ability to elicit an immune response.
A drug that lowers the body's normal immune response.
The condition of being pressed closely together and firmly fixed.
etymology: From Latin impingere (“to dash against, impinge”).

definition: The act of piercing with a sharpened stake as a form of punishment or torture.
etymology: From Middle French empalement; equivalent to impale + -ment.

definition: In an impassive manner.
example: He submitted impassively to his arrest.

definition: Painting that applies the pigment thickly so that brush or palette knife marks are visible.
Aspect without regard to the beginning or completion of the action of the verb.
Aspect without regard to the beginning or completion of the action of the verb.
Not perforated; having no opening.
example: Imperforate anus.

definition: A congenital defect of the anus; there is partial or complete obstruction of the anal opening.
Hymen that is completely closed so that menstrual blood cannot flow out.
In an imperious manner.
example: Imperiously he cut her short.

definition: Not permissibly.
example: The radon level in the basement was impermissibly high.

definition: Not easily perturbed or excited or upset; marked by extreme calm and composure.
example: Hitherto imperturbable, he now showed signs of alarm.
etymology: PIE word *né From Late Middle English imperturbable (“undisturbed;

definition: A very contagious infection of the skin; common in children; localized redness develops into small blisters that gradually crust and erode.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin impetīgō, from impetĕre (literally “to rush upon, assail, attack”).

definition: Unrighteousness by virtue of lacking respect for a god.
etymology: From Old French impieté, from Latin impietas, from in- (“not”) + pietas (“piety”), from pius (“pious, devout”) + -tās (“-ty, -dom”). By surface analysis, impious + -ety.

definition: The quality of provoking disbelief.
Not easy to believe.
Not politic.
example: An impolitic approach to a sensitive issue.

definition: The quality of lacking strength or power; being weak and feeble.
In a helpless manner.
Make poor.
example: That exuberant crop quickly impoverishes any fertile soil.
etymology: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

definition: Concerned with theoretical possibilities rather than actual use.
The quality of lacking precision.
The act of coercing someone into government service.
A lack of caution in practical affairs.
etymology: From im- + prudence. From Middle French imprudence, from Latin imprudentia.

definition: Attribute or credit to.
example: People impute great cleverness to cats.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).

definition: In an appositive manner.
Total lack of meaning or ideas.
etymology: From French inanité, from Latin inānitās (“emptiness”), equivalent to inane + -ity.

definition: Inappropriate conduct.
In an unarguable and undisputed manner.
In an inaudible manner.
example: She spoke inaudibly low.

definition: Lack of potential for development.
The act of inclining; bending forward.
example: An inclination of his head indicated his agreement.

definition: Something (usually a supporting document) that is enclosed in an envelope with a covering letter.
In an incompetent manner.
example: He did the job rather incompetently.

definition: To an inconceivable degree.
example: Inconceivably small.

definition: In an incongruous manner.
example: His shirttails stuck out from his tuxedo pants somewhat incongruously.

definition: In a manner intended to avoid attracting attention.
example: He had entered the room inconspicuously.

definition: Incapable of being contested or disputed.
example: That he was the greatest 100m runner of his generation was incontestable.

definition: Lack of conformity to social expectations.
To an incurable degree.
example: She was incurably optimistic.

definition: A council at which indigenous peoples of southern Africa meet to discuss some important question.
etymology: Borrowed from Zulu índaba (“affair, issue, matter; piece of news; story”), from ín- (class 9 noun prefix) + -daɓa (stem meaning ‘affair, matter’).

definition: In violation of good taste even verging on the indecent.
example: An indelicate remark.

definition: Freedom from control or influence of another or others.
In an indigenous manner.
Antonyms whose opposition is mediated (e.g., the antonymy of ‘wet’ and ‘parched’ is mediated by the similarity of ‘parched’ to ‘dry’).
Indirect procedure or action.
example: He tried to find out by indirection.

definition: Difficult or impossible to perceive or discern.
example: An indiscernible increase in temperature.

definition: A slight illness.
etymology: From Middle English indisposicioun, from Middle French indisposicion.

definition: (of a substance) incapable of being dissolved.
example: It connected in one indissoluble bond.
etymology: From Middle French indissoluble, from Latin indissolubilis.

definition: Discriminating the individual from the generic group or species.
Make or mark or treat as individual.
example: The sounds were individualized by sharpness and tone.

definition: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (trade name Indocin).
In an indulgent manner.

example: The baby's heart was pulsating again after the surgeon massaged it.

definition: Bread made of coarse rye flour.
Marked by precise accordance with details.
example: Punctilious in his attention to rules of etiquette.
etymology: From punctilio (“fine point in exactness of conduct”) + -ous.

definition: A one-horse sleigh consisting of a box on runners.
etymology: Shortened form of tom-pung, from the same Algonquian etymon as toboggan.

definition: Wit having a sharp and caustic quality.
example: He commented with typical pungency.

definition: Develop into a pupa.
example: The insect larva pupate.

definition: Reflex contraction of the sphincter muscle of the iris in response to a bright light (or certain drugs) causing the pupil to become smaller.
A ring of smooth muscle surrounding the iris.
Having a list of ancestors as proof of being a purebred animal.
Being undiluted or unmixed with extraneous material.
Strongly laxative.
Scrupulous or exaggerated insistence on purity or correctness (especially in language).
example: Linguistic purisms.
etymology: From French purisme. By surface analysis, pur(e) + -ism.

definition: North American orchid having a spike of violet-purple flowers mixed with white; sepals and petals form a hood.
Having or showing or acting with a purpose or design.
example: Purposive behavior.

definition: A plant of the family Portulacaceae having fleshy succulent obovate leaves often grown as a potherb or salad herb; a weed in some areas.
Containing pus.
example: A purulent wound.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French purulent, from Latin pūrulentus, from pūs (“pus”).

definition: Lacking in courage and manly strength and resolution; contemptibly fearful.
example: The soldier deserted his troop in a pusillanimous manner.

definition: To go stealthily or furtively.
etymology: From pussy (“feline”) + foot; because of the light and careful tread of cats.

definition: The smallest monkey; of tropical forests of the Amazon.
Relating to or near the pylorus.

A pale yellow crystalline hydrocarbon C16H10 extracted from coal tar.
A B vitamin that is essential for metabolism of amino acids and starch.
A person with a mania for setting things on fire.
Any of a group of crystalline silicate mineral common in igneous and metamorphic rocks.

definition: Fruit of such plants as the plantain; a capsule whose upper part falls off when the seeds are released.
etymology: From Latin pyxis (“small box”). Doublet of box, piseog, and pyx.

definition: An Islamic judge.
etymology: From Arabic قَاضٍ (qāḍin, “judge”). Doublet of alcalde, casis, cauzee, and kadhi.

definition: The leaves of the shrub Catha edulis which are chewed like tobacco or used to make tea; has the effect of a euphoric stimulant.
The direction of the Kaaba toward which Muslims turn for their daily prayers.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic قِبْلَة (qibla, “which is opposite”).

definition: A cubelike object.
etymology: From Middle English quadrat, quadrate, from Latin quadrātum. Doublet of quadrat; compare also quadrant (“square or quadrangle”).

definition: Paralysis of both arms and both legs.
etymology: From quadri- (“four”) + -plegia, from Ancient Greek πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike”); probably patterned after paraplegia.

definition: A hearty draft.
etymology: Uncertain. Suggestions include connection with Old Irish cuäch (“cup, goblet, bowl; cauldron, large vessel; bowl, cup”) (whence Scots quaich, queff). The noun is derived from the verb.

definition: Mammal of South Africa that resembled a zebra; extinct since late 19th century.
etymology: From Dutch quagga (whence also Afrikaans kwagga), from a Khoisan term, probably Haiǁom, Khoekhoe ǁkoaah, apparently of imitative origin.

definition: Atlantic coast round clams with hard shells; large clams usually used for chowders or other clam dishes.
etymology: Most often thought to be from Narragansett poquaûhock (“hard clam”), or perhaps from pohkeni (“dark”) + hogki (“shell”). Alternatively from Mohegan-Pequot p'quaghhaug (“hard clam”) or another Algonquian language.

definition: In a strange but not unpleasant manner.
example: The old lady expressed herself somewhat quaintly.

definition: Uneasiness about the fitness of an action (particularly for reasons of ethics, morals or propriety).
example: This lawyer has no qualms about saving people who are on the wrong side of the law.

definition: A homogeneous polynomial having at least two variables.
An algebraic equation or function of the fourth degree.
A polynomial of the fourth degree.
The cardinal number that is the sum of three and one.
etymology: From Middle English quaterniǒun, from Late Latin quaterniō, from quaternī (“four each”) + -iō, from quater (“four times”). Doublet of kern.

definition: (of the voice) quivering as from weakness or fear.
example: The old lady's quavering voice.

definition: Australian timber tree resembling the kauri but having wood much lighter in weight and softer.
A white crystalline oxide used in the production of calcium hydroxide.
etymology: From Middle English quyk lym; equivalent to quick + lime.

definition: Hurried repair.
Euphemisms for death (based on an analogy between lying in a bed and in a tomb).
etymology: Short for Medieval Latin quiētus est (literally “he is quiet”). First attested in the 1530s. Earlier attested as Late Middle English quietus est. Doublet of coy, quiet, quit, and quite.

definition: Any of a class of aromatic yellow compounds including several that are biologically important as coenzymes or acceptors or vitamins; used in making dyes.
etymology: From quinic acid + -one, since it is one of the compounds obtained upon oxidation of quinic acid.

definition: The number that is represented as a one followed by 18 zeros in the US.
etymology: From French quintillion. By surface analysis, quint- (“five”) + -illion.

definition: Document transferring title or right or claim to another.
etymology: From Middle English quiteclaymen, from Anglo-Norman quiteclamer, from clamer quite (“to claim quit”). Compare claim quit.

definition: Document transferring title or right or claim to another.
In a quizzical and questioning manner.

definition: Rabbis collectively.
A political leader who seeks support by appealing to popular passions and prejudices.
Usually elongate cluster of flowers along the main stem in which the flowers at the base open first.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin racēmus (“cluster, bunch”). Doublet of raisin.

definition: Discriminatory or abusive behavior towards members of another race.
etymology: From racial + -ism. Coined in 1882 based on the older use of "race" as a synonym of "nation, tribe, ethnic group", later senses (from 1890) from the use of "race" for racial categories.

definition: A person with a prejudiced belief that one racial group is superior to others.
In a radiant manner.
example: The bride smiled radiantly.

definition: Prized variety of chicory having globose heads of red leaves.
In a radioactive manner.
example: Radioactively labeled.

definition: A photographic image produced on a radiosensitive surface by radiation other than visible light (especially by X-rays or gamma rays).
A person who makes radiographs.
A dirty shabbily clothed urchin.
etymology: From the Middle English Ragamuffyn. Of uncertain origin, according to Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable: A muffin is a poor thing of a creature, a ‘regular muff’; so that a ragamuffin is a sorry creature in rags.

definition: Fringed orchid of the eastern United States having a greenish flower with the lip deeply lacerated.
East Indian cereal grass whose seed yield a somewhat bitter flour, a staple in the Orient.
Well-seasoned stew of meat and vegetables.
etymology: Borrowed from French ragoût. Compare ragù of the same origin, borrowed from Italian.

definition: Widespread European weed having yellow daisylike flowers; sometimes an obnoxious weed and toxic to cattle if consumed in quantity.

definition: A railroad depot in a theater of operations where military supplies are unloaded for distribution.
Malayan tree bearing spiny red fruit.

definition: Malayan tree bearing spiny red fruit.
The act of branching out or dividing into branches.
etymology: From Middle French ramification, or its source, Medieval Latin rāmificātiō. By surface analysis, ramify + -ication.

definition: A simple type of jet engine; must be launched at high speed.
A simple type of jet engine; must be launched at high speed.
Showing deep-seated resentment.
example: Preserve … from rancorous envy of the rich.

definition: Arrange in random order.
example: Randomize the order of the numbers.

definition: Tall and thin and having long slender limbs.
example: For an accountant, Robert had a rangy appearance.

definition: A histamine blocker and antacid (trade name Zantac) used to treat peptic ulcers and gastritis and esophageal reflux.
A commissioned officer who has been promoted from enlisted status.
A ridge that forms a seam between two parts.
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin raphē, from Ancient Greek ῥᾰφή (rhăphḗ, “seam; suture”).

definition: In an ecstatic manner.
Having low density.
Playful in an appealingly bold way.
The trait of acting rashly and without prudence.
Liable to payment of locally assessed property taxes.
Of or relating to the philosophical doctrine of rationalism.
Living by preying on other animals especially by catching living prey.

definition: Small flower with a flat strap-shaped corolla usually occupying the peripheral rings of a composite flower.

etymology: Uncertain; perhaps an extended form of razz(le-dazzle). Compare pizzazz. Earliest citation from 1888, as razz-ma-taz.

definition: A handbook of tables used to facilitate computation.

definition: Capable of being realized.

Someone who reasons logically.
Awaken once again.

The act of calculating again (usually to eliminate errors or to include additional data).
example: Recalculation yielded a much larger value.

definition: A disavowal or taking back of a previous assertion.
Summarize briefly.
example: Let's recapitulate the main ideas.

definition: Reconnaissance (by shortening).
The withdrawal of the clergy and choir from the chancel to the vestry at the end of a church service.
A march to be played for processions.
Of or pertaining to a recession.
Someone who is repeatedly arrested for criminal behavior (especially for the same criminal behavior).
etymology: From French récidiviste, from Latin recidīvus (“returning, recurring”). Compare recidivous, -ist. By surface analysis, recidive + -ist.

definition: An expert at calculation (or at operating calculating machines).
etymology: From Middle English reknere, rekenere. Cognate with Afrikaans rekenaar, Dutch Low Saxon rekener, German Rechner, Danish regner, Swedish räknare. By surface analysis, reckon + -er.

definition: Converting from one code to another.
Of or being a weapon that is designed to minimize recoil.
Bring into an improved condition.

definition: Explore, often with the goal of finding something or somebody.

definition: Explore, often with the goal of finding something or somebody.
example: Our scout will reconnoitre the path ahead of our troops.
etymology: From French reconnoître (obsolete spelling of reconnaître), from Latin recognoscere (“to recognise”). There is also an obsolete 19th-century British English spelling reconnaitre, influenced by the modern French form.

etymology: Middle French reconquerir, reconquérir or from re- + conquer.

New Zealand tree with glossy leaves and scaly reddish-brown bark.
Any of several voles of mountainous regions of Eurasia and America.

Low tropical American shrub having powerful emetic properties.

definition: Low tropical American shrub having powerful emetic properties.
A speedy red or red-and-tan American hound.
Small Old World songbird with a reddish breast.

definition: Of or relating to British universities founded in the late 19th century or the 20th century.
(British informal) a provincial British university of relatively recent founding; distinguished from Oxford University and Cambridge University.
Small shrubby tree of eastern North America similar to the Judas tree having usually pink flowers; found in damp sheltered underwood.
A member of the military police in Britain.

definition: British soldier; so-called because of the soldier's red coat (especially during the American Revolution).
Dedicate anew.

example: The rededication of the Temple of Jerusalem.

definition: Small but gamy pickerel of Atlantic coastal states.
A draft for the amount of a dishonored draft plus the costs and charges of drafting again.
Flycatching warbler of eastern North America the male having bright orange on sides and wings and tail.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English *redstert; equivalent to red + start (“tail”). Compare Dutch roodstaart, Danish rødstjert.

definition: Elect again.
Give a new surface.
example: Refinish the dining room furniture.

definition: The phenomenon of a propagating wave (light or sound) being thrown back from a surface.
etymology: From Middle English reflexion, reflexioun, from Middle French reflexion and its etymon Late Latin reflexiō; the variant spelling reflection is due to influence from correction.

definition: The coreferential relation between a reflexive pronoun and its antecedent.
A doctrine of reform.
Subject to refraction.
example: Refract a light beam.
etymology: From Latin refrāctum, neuter form of refrāctus, the past participle of refringō, itself from re- (“again”) + frangō (“to break”).

definition: In a regal manner.

etymology: From Middle English regali; equivalent to regal + -ly.

definition: The imposition of order or discipline.
A serious chronic and progressive inflammation of the ileum producing frequent bouts of diarrhea with abdominal pain and nausea and fever and weight loss.
A dodecahedron with twelve regular pentagons as faces.
An icosahedron with twenty equilateral triangles as faces.
Bring into conformity with rules or principles or usage; impose regulations.
example: We cannot regulate the way people dress.

definition: Restricting according to rules or principles.
example: A regulatory gene.

definition: Regarding something abstract as a material thing.
etymology: First attested around 1846; a macaronic calque of German Verdinglichung, using -ification (“making”) for ver- + -lich + -ung, and Latin rēs (“thing”) for Ding (“thing”)

definition: Any of several American wildflowers with a kidney-shaped lip.
Hormone secreted by the corpus luteum during the last days of pregnancy; relaxes the pelvic ligaments and prepares the uterus for labor.
With relevance.
Piety by virtue of being devout.
A verbal act of renouncing a claim or right or position etc.
The act of expressing earnest opposition or protest.
Argue in protest or opposition.
etymology: From (the participle stem of) Late Latin remōnstrō, from Latin re- + mōnstrō.

definition: Marine fishes with a flattened elongated body and a sucking disk on the head for attaching to large fish or moving objects.
Without pity; in a merciless manner.
For which money is paid.
example: Remunerative work.

That is able or fit be rented.
example: That apartment isn't rentable because it failed its building inspection.

definition: Someone whose income is from property rents or bond interest and other investments.
The food served and eaten at one time.
etymology: From Middle English repast, repaste (“feast, meal; food, nourishment; the Eucharist;

definition: A race (especially in rowing) in which runners-up in the eliminating heats compete for a place in the final race.
etymology: From French repêchage, from repêcher (“to fish out, rescue”), from re- (“again”) + pêcher (“to fish”).

definition: Verboseness resulting from excessive repetitions.
Changing a particular word or phrase.
Put in a new, usually larger, pot.
example: The plant had grown and had to be repotted.

definition: Expressible in symbolic form.
example: Uniquely representable in the form ….

definition: Use again after processing.
An act or expression of criticism and censure.
etymology: From Old French reprove, from reprover. See reprove.

definition: Take to task.
example: She ached to be with Affad again – and to reprove the feeling she frowned and bit her lip.
etymology: From Middle English repreven, reproven, from Anglo-Norman reprover, Middle French reprouver, from Latin reprobāre. Doublet of reprobate.

definition: The act of publishing again.
Intense aversion.
example: Moral repugnance.
etymology: From Middle English repugnance, repugnaunce, from Old French repugnance, repugnaunce (French répugnance) and its etymon Latin repugnantia. Doublet of repugnancy.

definition: A painted or carved screen placed above and behind an altar or communion table.
etymology: From Middle English reredos, from Anglo-Norman reredos, areredos; equivalent to rere (“rear”) + French dos (“back”).

definition: A reply by a Pope to an inquiry concerning a point of law or morality.
Seal again.
example: Reseal the bottle after using the medicine.

definition: The 20th letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
etymology: From Proto-Semitic *raʾš- (“head”). Doublet of ras (“Ethiopian king”) and ras (“headland”), and related to reis.

definition: Entitled to the residue of an estate (after payment of debts and specific gifts).
example: The residuary part of the estate.

definition: Someone who systematically obstructs some action that others want to take.
Capable of being solved.
A person who respects someone or something; usually used in the negative.
example: X is no respecter of Y.

definition: Breathe easily again, as after exertion or anxiety.
etymology: From Middle English respiren, borrowed from Old French respirer or Latin respīrō (“to blow back, breathe out”), from re- (“back”) + spīrō (“to breathe, blow”).

definition: Any of the enzymes that cut nucleic acid at specific restriction sites and produce restriction fragments; obtained from bacteria (where they cripple viral invaders); used in recombinant DNA technology.
The phenomenon of resistance to motion through a fluid.
Network of tubules carrying sperm from the seminiferous tubules to the vasa efferentia.
Form a net or a network.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin rēticulātus (“reticulated, net-like”).

definition: (photography) the formation of a network of cracks or wrinkles in a photographic emulsion.
example: The students studied the reticulation of the veins in the leaf.
etymology: By surface analysis, reticule + -ation, or, by surface analysis, reticulate + -ion.

definition: A woman's drawstring handbag; usually made of net or beading or brocade; used in 18th and 19th centuries.
etymology: From French réticule, from Latin rēticulum, diminutive of rēte (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticulum, and Reticulum.

Transmit again.

definition: Capable of being regained especially with effort.
example: He believed the information was retrievable.

definition: Reference to things past.
example: The story begins with no introductory retrospections.

definition: Unify again, as of a country.
example: Will Korea reunify?

definition: Disposed to seek revenge or intended for revenge.
Spread negative information about.
etymology: From Middle English revilen, from re + Old French aviler (“to make vile or cheap, disprize, disesteem”), from a- (“to”) + vil (“vile, cheap”); see vile.

definition: Tending to impart new life and vigor to.
An attempt to reawaken the evangelical faith.
example: Art Deco revivalism.

definition: A radical supporter of political or social revolution.
Changing a particular word or phrase.
A highly malignant neoplasm derived from striated muscle.
Feeling great rapture or delight.
etymology: From Latinized form of Ancient Greek ῥαψῳδῐκός (rhapsōidĭkós).

Of or relating to rheology.
A person who delivers a speech or oration.

etymology: From Middle English rethoricien, from Old French retoricien; equivalent to rhetoric + -ian.

definition: Any of a group of picornaviruses that are responsible for many upper respiratory infections.
A red photopigment in the retinal rods of vertebrates; dissociates into retinene by light.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon, “rose”), due to its pinkish color, and ὄψις (ópsis, “sight”).

definition: A parallelogram with adjacent sides of unequal lengths; an oblique-angled parallelogram with only the opposite sides equal.
Any of several muscles of the upper back that help move the shoulder blade.
Syncopated music in duple time for dancing the rumba.
A writer who composes rhymes; a maker of poor verses (usually used as terms of contempt for minor or inferior poets).

definition: A transferase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of ribonucleic acid.
A gaping grimace.
example: His face was a rictus of sheer delight.

definition: An antibacterial drug (trade names Rifadin and Rimactane) used to treat tuberculosis.
Tubular pasta in short ribbed pieces.

definition: A set of confused and meaningless statements.

etymology: From ragman roll (“long list; catalogue”). Recorded since c1736.

definition: A small stream.

definition: The opening through which food is taken in and vocalizations emerge.
Lacking a rim or frame.
example: Rimless glasses.

example: Pull the ripcord.

definition: Arousing or provoking laughter.
example: Risible courtroom antics.

definition: A protease inhibitor (trade name Norvir) used in treating HIV.
A small stream.
example: A rivulet of tears ran down his face.
etymology: From Italian rivoletto, diminutive of rivolo (“trickle, little stream”), diminutive of rivo (“stream, brook, creek”), ultimately from Latin rīvulus, diminutive of rīvus. By surface analysis, Latin rīvus + -ule + -et.

definition: A workman who is employed to repair roads.
A driver who obstructs others.
Lacking pathways.
example: Roadless areas.

definition: Someone who leads a wandering unsettled life.
Small Old World songbird with a reddish breast.
etymology: From the name Robin + redbreast. See robin.

definition: An phone call made by an automated service.
etymology: From robo- + call. First use appears c. 1998 in the Associated Press Newswire.

Be agitated.

A conveyance that transports passengers or freight in carriers suspended from cables and supported by a series of towers.
Of or resembling rope (or ropes) in being long and strong.
Of something having a dusty purplish pink color.

A cruel and brutal fellow.

definition: The basic unit of money in Belarus.

definition: A form of football played with an oval ball.

definition: A person who destroys or ruins or lays waste to.
A substantial increase over a relatively short period of time.

definition: The large yellow root of a rutabaga plant used as food.

definition: A cruciferous plant with a thick bulbous edible yellow root.

A rapid, jerky movement of the eyes between positions of rest.
An officer of the church who is in charge of sacred objects.
etymology: From French sacristain, Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer. Doublet of sexton.

definition: A long narrow feather on the back (saddle) of a domestic fowl.

etymology: From Middle English viscountes, viscountesse, probably from Middle French viscontesse; equivalent to viscount + -ess. Doublet of vicomtesse.

definition: A percept that arises from the eyes; an image in the visual system.
One whose prevailing mental imagery is visual.
(philosophy) a doctrine that life is a vital principle distinct from physics and chemistry.
Corrupt morally or by intemperance or sensuality.
etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Latin vitiātus, the perfect passive participle of vitiō (“damage, spoil”), from vitium (“vice”).

definition: Impaired by diminution.
A vitrified substance; the glassy result of being vitrified.
etymology: From Late Latin *vitrificātio (“glassification”), from *vitrificāre (“to glassify”), from vitrum (“glass”) + -ificāre (“-ify”). Cf. French vitrification, Spanish vitrificación, Italian vitrificazione.

definition: (of tempo) very fast and lively.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian vivace (“brisk, lively”), from Latin vīvāx (“lively, vigorous, energetic”), from vīvō (“live, be alive”).

definition: An indoor enclosure for keeping and raising living animals and plants and observing them under natural conditions.
Producing living young (not eggs).
etymology: From Latin vīviparus, from vīvus (“alive, life, living”) + pariō (“give birth, produce, bring forth”).

definition: Hungarian hunting dog resembling the Weimaraner but having a rich deep red coat.
Sing (each note a scale or in a melody) with the same vowel.
Relating to a case used in some languages.
example: Vocative verb endings.
etymology: From Late Middle English [Term?], borrowed from Middle French vocatif, from Latin vocātīvus (“for calling”); a calque of Ancient Greek κλητῐκή (klētĭkḗ, “for calling;

definition: The case (in some inflected languages) used when the referent of the noun is being addressed.
Capable of being rescinded or voided.
example: Voidable contracts.

definition: An organ stop producing a gentle tremolo effect.
With wings extended in a flying position.
etymology: From Middle French volant, present participle of voler (“to fly”), from Latin volāre.

definition: Relating to the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot.
example: The volar surface.

definition: The branch of geology that studies volcanoes.
etymology: From French volcanologie, from volcan (“volcano”); and/or directly from volcano + -logy.

definition: With deliberate intention.
example: A volitional act.

definition: Ornament consisting of a curve on a plane that winds around a center with an increasing distance from the center.
etymology: From French volute, from Italian voluta, from Latin volūta, from the feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Doublet of vault.

definition: A spring in the shape of a coil.
Process of treating rubber or rubberlike materials with sulphur at great heat to improve elasticity and strength or to harden them.
Of or relating to the vulva.
The fissure between the labia majora.
Any of many long-legged birds that wade in water in search of food.
Panel forming the lower part of an interior wall when it is finished differently from the rest of the wall.
A buoyant board (resembling a surfboard) that is used to ride over water while being pulled behind a motorboat.
Carefully observant or attentive; on the lookout for possible danger.
An easy victory.
example: There had been several walkaways from the juvenile center.

definition: A wide flat board used to cover walls or partitions; made from plaster or wood pulp or other materials and used primarily to form the interior walls of houses.
A politician who belongs to a small clique that controls a political party for private rather than public ends.
Military quarters for dining and recreation for officers of a warship (except the captain).
example: The captain rarely referred to his wardroom for advice, and this resulted in their discontent.

definition: Marked by warmth of feeling like kindness and sympathy and generosity.
example: Gave a warmhearted welcome to the stranger.

definition: A bathroom sink that is permanently installed and connected to a water supply and drainpipe; where you can wash your hands and face.
A working woman who takes in washing.
Celebrate noisily, often indulging in drinking; engage in uproarious festivities.
example: The next morning he much regretted the gusto with which he had wassailed the night before.
etymology: From Middle English wassail, from Old Norse ves heill (“be healthy!”), from the imperative of vesa (“to be”) + heill (“healthy”).

definition: To a wasteful manner or to a wasteful degree.
etymology: From Middle English wastfully; equivalent to wasteful + -ly.

definition: The trait of wasting resources.
example: A life characterized by thriftlessness and waste.
etymology: From Middle English wastfulnes; equivalent to wasteful + -ness.

definition: A container with an open top; for discarded paper and other rubbish.
Someone who dissipates resources self-indulgently.
The process of paying close and continuous attention.
example: Wakefulness, watchfulness, and bellicosity make a good hunter.

definition: Small Indian lettuce of northern regions.
Plant of ponds and slow streams having submerged and floating leaves and white flowers; Europe and North America.
Eurasia; northern North America to Virginia.
Plant of wet places in Eurasia and America.
Not permitting the passage of water.
A tornado passing over water and picking up a column of water and mist.
A wheel with buckets attached to its rim; raises water from a stream or pond.
Floating aquatic carnivorous perennial of central and southern Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia having whorls of 6 to 9 leaves ending in hinged lobes for capturing e.g. water fleas.
Twining shrub of North America having yellow capsules enclosing scarlet seeds.
A receipt given by the carrier to the shipper acknowledging receipt of the goods being shipped and specifying the terms of delivery.
Traveling especially on foot.
example: A poor wayfaring stranger.
etymology: From Middle English wayferande, weyverinde, wayverinde, from Old English weġfarende, weġfērende (“wayfaring”), equivalent to way + faring. Cognate with Icelandic vegfarandi. More at wayfare.

definition: Vigorous deciduous European treelike shrub common along waysides; red berries turn black.
So lacking in interest as to cause mental weariness.
example: Other people's dreams are dreadfully wearisome.
etymology: From Middle English werisom, equivalent to weary + -some.

definition: Producing exhaustion.
A long thin board with one edge thicker than the other; used as siding by lapping one board over the board below.
Mechanical device attached to an elevated structure; rotates freely to show the direction of the wind.
Ski, alternating directions.
A white person, who is obsessed with Japanese culture, usually pejorative.
A hand tool for removing weeds.
A chemical agent that destroys plants or inhibits their growth.
Platform scale flush with a roadway for weighing vehicles and cattle etc.
The apparent surface of the imaginary sphere on which celestial bodies appear to be projected.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English welkne (“weather; heavens;

definition: American blackberry with oblong black fruit.
Perennial cottony-white herb of southwestern United States.
Shrub of western United States having pink or crimson flowers; often forms thickets.
Of western North America; male is black and yellow and orange-red.
Something especially big or impressive of its kind.
A person who is regarded as eccentric or mad.
A horny material from the upper jaws of certain whales; used as the ribs of fans or as stays in corsets.
Whale with plates of whalebone along the upper jaw for filtering plankton from the water.
Beat with force.
example: I ought to have whanged him one in the eye.

definition: Hit hard.
example: She whapped down on the floor.

definition: A field planted with wheat.
Influence or urge by gentle urging, caressing, or flattering.
example: I’d like one of those, too, if you can wheedle him into telling you where he got it.
etymology: Uncertain. Perhaps continuing Middle English wedlen (“to beg, ask for alms”), from Old English wǣdlian (“to be poor, be needy, be in want, beg”), from Proto-Germanic *wēþlōną (“to be in need”).

definition: Large marine snail much used as food in Europe.
etymology: From Middle English whelke, from Old English hwelca (“pustule, swelling”).

definition: Sailing barge used especially in East Anglia.
example: He went out for Freshman rowing but didn't make any of the crews and took to rowing by himself in a wherry three afternoons a week.
etymology: From Middle English whery (“small boat”), of obscure origin but cognate to French houari and Breton ouari, as well as Welsh chweri (“small boat”).

definition: The characteristic sounds made by a horse.
etymology: From Middle English whynyen, whinien, akin to Middle English whinen (“to whine”).

definition: Someone who is unimportant but cheeky and presumptuous.
example: These whippersnappers have never had to walk far or carry water.
etymology: Extension of *whip-snapper (“a cracker of whips”), or perhaps from snipper-snapper. Compare also whipperginnie (“term of abuse for a woman”), late 16th c.

definition: Bending and snapping back readily without breaking.
example: The tree's whippy branches grazed his face.

definition: A conical child's plaything tapering to a steel point on which it can be made to spin.
etymology: From Middle English whyrlegygge; equivalent to whirl (noun or verb) + gig (“a top”).

definition: Aquatic beetle that circles rapidly on the water surface.
etymology: So called due to its behavior of spinning rapidly in place when alarmed, in a manner similar to a whirligig or spinning top.

definition: Having hair on the cheeks and chin.
example: Michael's heavily whiskered face hadn't seen a razor in some days.

definition: California herb with white conic or bell-shaped flowers usually tinged with green.
North American plant having large leaves and yellowish green flowers growing in racemes; yields a toxic alkaloid used medicinally.
Having blotches of white.
Easily frightened.
Minnows or other small fresh- or saltwater fish (especially herring); usually cooked whole.
A person who is inwardly evil but outwardly professes to be virtuous.
etymology: An allusion to Matthew 23:27 in the Bible. From Ancient Greek τάφος κεκονιαμένος (táphos kekoniaménos, “plastered tomb, hypocrite”).

definition: Hardy English breed of cattle raised extensively in United States.
example: Whiteface is sometimes worn by clowns and mimes, or in the Gothic subculture.

definition: Minute insect that feeds on plant juices; related to scale insects.
An agent that makes things white or colorless.
Largest hare of northern plains and western mountains of United States; brownish-grey in summer and pale grey in winter; tail nearly always all white.
Light easily worked wood of a tulip tree; used for furniture and veneer.
A purulent infection at the end of a finger or toe in the area surrounding the nail.
Annual weed of Europe and North America having a rosette of basal leaves and tiny flowers followed by oblong seed capsules.
etymology: Supposed to cure whitlow, a nail infection.

definition: Hit with the hand.
example: If you don’t cut that out, I’m going to whomp you so hard your head will spin!
etymology: Perhaps a variant of whip, similar to whup.

definition: Prepare or cook quickly or hastily.
example: Why don't I just whomp up some scrambled eggs while you're waiting?

definition: Strike hard.
example: He angrily whopped the book onto the table.
etymology: From Middle English whappen, a variant of wappen (“to strike; fling; shoot; stun”), probably of imitative origin. Compare Old Norse vappa (“to waddle”).

definition: Befitting or characteristic of a wife.
etymology: From Middle English wifly, wyfly, from Old English wīflīc (“womanly, wifely”), from Proto-Germanic *wībalīkaz (“wifely”).

definition: Wearing a wig.
example: The judges all wigged and robed.

definition: Coarse erect biennial Old World herb introduced as a weed in eastern North America.
Perennial purple-flowered wild mallow of western North America that is also cultivated.
Common perennial United States spurge having showy white petallike bracts.
Slender and graceful.
Used especially of trees; growing in a shape determined by the prevailing winds.
Hedge or fence of trees designed to lessen the force of the wind and reduce erosion.
example: I built my windbreak on a second-story wooden deck, as you can see above, but it would work just as well at ground level.

definition: Without or almost without wind.
example: He prefers windless days for playing golf.
etymology: From Middle English wyndles, equivalent to wind + -less. Cognate with Old Norse vindlauss (“windless”).

definition: A glass that has a stem and in which wine is served.
A heel on a woman's shoe in the shape of a wineglass.
Separate the chaff from grain by using air currents.
example: She stood there winnowing grain all day in the field.

definition: Dismiss from consideration or a contest.
Small Old World perennial herb grown for its bright yellow flowers which appear in early spring often before snow is gone.
European herb with vanilla-scented white-pink flowers.
Succulent herb sometimes grown as a salad or pot herb; grows on dunes and waste ground of Pacific coast of North America.
Witty remark.
A sadly pensive longing.
Strong flexible twig.
A message whose ingenuity or verbal skill or incongruity has the power to evoke laughter.
etymology: From witty + -icism; coined in the 1670s by John Dryden, by analogy to criticism.

definition: With full knowledge and deliberation.
example: He wittingly deleted the references.
etymology: From Middle English wetandly, wettanly, wetyngly, witandly, witingeliche, wittandly, wittingli, wittingly, wityngli, wityngly, witynly, wytindeliche, wytyngly, equivalent to witting + -ly. Cognate with German wissentlich.

definition: Take (someone) as a wife.
etymology: From Middle English wiven, iwiven, from Old English wīfian, wīfiġan, ġewīfian (“to take a wife; marry”).

definition: A blue dyestuff obtained from the woad plant.
etymology: From Middle English wode, from Old English wād (“woad”), from Proto-West Germanic *waiʀd, from Proto-Germanic *waizdaz (“woad”), from Proto-Indo-European *woydʰ-.

definition: Something that wobbles.
The largest breed of dogs; formerly used to hunt wolves.
Poisonous Eurasian perennial herb with broad rounded leaves and yellow flowers and fibrous rootstock.
etymology: From wolf + -s- + bane, a calque of Ancient Greek λυκοκτόνον (lukoktónon), from λύκος (lúkos, “wolf”) + κτείνω (kteínō, “to kill”). Influenced by Latin lycoctonum.

definition: A man who likes many women and has short sexual relationships with them.
(used as an intensifier) excellently.
example: The colors changed wondrously slowly.

definition: Eurasia except southern Russia; northern North America.
European perennial herb with greenish yellow terminal flower clusters.
etymology: Named for its natural habitat, the undergrowth of woods and forests.

definition: A carving created by carving wood.
Texture produced by the fibers in wood.
A pile or stack of wood to be used for fuel.
Move with a sibilant sound.
A fellow worker.
example: He loved going to the boozer for lunch with his workmates.

definition: In a worried manner.
example: ‘I wonder what to do,’ she said worriedly.

definition: In a worthy manner; with worthiness.
etymology: From Middle English worthely, worthili, worthiliche, worthily, worthyly, worþili, worþiliche, worþily, wurðelice, wurðeliche, wurðelike, wurthelie, wurthilyche, wurthyly, equivalent to worthy + -ly.

definition: In a wretched manner.
example: ‘I can't remember who I am,’ I said, wretchedly.
etymology: From Middle English wrecchedly; equivalent to wretched + -ly.

definition: A band or bracelet worn around the wrist.
etymology: From wrist + -let (suffix indicating a piece of an object).

definition: A person who transgresses moral or civil law.
example: Get and keep wrongdoers out of your thorp (village).

definition: Obstinately perverse in judgment or opinion.
example: A wrongheaded policy.

definition: Crystalline oxidation product of the metabolism of nucleoproteins; precursor of uric acid; found in many organs and in urine.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, from French xanthine, reflecting New Latin combining forms: xanth- + -ine; ultimately from Ancient Greek ξανθός (xanthós, “yellow”), because xanthine is yellowish-white.

definition: Being four more than forty.
Noisy talk.
example: If 't ash tree buds before 't yack, […].

definition: Talk incessantly and tiresomely.
Noisy talk.
A skullcap worn by religious Jews (especially at prayer).
etymology: Borrowed from Yiddish יאַרמלקע (yarmlke), from Polish jarmułka (“skullcap”), from Turkic; compare Turkish yağmurluk (“rain apparel”).

definition: Of or resembling or containing yeast.
Common weedy and bristly grass found in nearly all temperate areas.
A kind of gurnard.
Poisonous woody evergreen vine of southeastern United States having fragrant yellow funnel-shaped flowers.
An impure mixture of uranium oxides obtained during the processing of uranium ore.
etymology: From yellow + cake, from its colour and texture.

definition: A fish of the Pacific coast of North America.
Stoloniferous herb of southwestern United States and Mexico having a pungent rootstock and small spicate flowers with white bracts suggesting an anemone.
A cruel and brutal fellow.
etymology: Backslang for boy. The second sense was likely influenced by hobnob and/or yokel.

definition: A cruel and brutal fellow.
Stupid and ignorant like proverbial rural inhabitants.
example: The boy's empty yokel-like expression.

definition: Capable of fathering offspring.
A soft silvery metallic element; a rare earth of the lanthanide series; it occurs in gadolinite and monazite and xenotime.
etymology: From Ytterby + -ium, named after Ytterby, Sweden. Doublet of erbium, terbium, and yttrium

definition: A Common Slavonic nasal vowel in the early Cyrillic and Glagolitic alphabets.
example: The names of the letters do not imply capitalization, as both little and big yus exist in majuscule and minuscule variants.

definition: Excessive intolerance of opposing views.
Yellow carotenoid (isomeric with lutein and occurs widely with it) that is the main pigment in yellow Indian corn.
etymology: From New Latin Zea (genus name of Indian corn) + xanthin.

definition: Domesticated ox having a humped back and long horns and a large dewlap; used chiefly as a draft animal in India and east Asia.
etymology: Borrowed from French zébu, probably from Tibetan མཛོ་པོ (mdzo po, “male bull–yak hybrid”), whence also zobo.

definition: Preceding even the first.
example: The zeroth order polynomial approximation is constant.

definition: A toxic salt of selenous acid and zinc, with the chemical formula ZnSeO3 ….
example: Zinc selenite is used in the glass industry.

definition: Medium-sized tubular pasta in short pieces.
etymology: From Italian zite or ziti, plural of zita, zito, from a Southern (Neapolitan or Sicilian) word likely from Vulgar Latin pittitus (“small, worthless”), originally denoting a young boy or girl. See also petty.

definition: Music of southern Louisiana that combines French dance melodies with Caribbean music and blues.
etymology: From Louisiana Creole zydéco, compare French zarico; possibly from a metanalysis of French les haricots (“beans”) as French le zarico (“beans”) in a dance-tune title.
